wetland_management__asset_threat__drough.mechanism: Drought damages the restored wetland by taking away the water it runs on. In a rewetted Indonesian peat restoration area, peat-surface subsidence accelerated sharply during and shortly after the 2019 El Niño drought when groundwater depths were very low, running 2.5 to 4 times the rate of the preceding 3.5 years and more than double the 7.5-year mean (ev_climate_shock_hooi24_5). The authors read their long record as showing that a severe drought could still cause major water-table drops to near 1 m below the peat surface, with carbon-emission spikes, even in otherwise rewetted conditions, in restoration areas and remaining peat-swamp forest alike (ev_climate_shock_hooi24_6). On a restored floodplain the hazard works by removing the flood the wetland depends on: in 2020, lack of snow cover and severe drought meant no spring flooding on the Pripyat floodplain, and migrating and nesting birds on the restored floodplain meadows declined strongly (ev_wgy_blr_6). The Ramsar technical guidance records, from its authors' knowledge, that a large number of planted areas in degraded tropical peat-swamp forest have been lost to drought, as well as to fire, flooding and out-competition by ferns and sedges (ev_wgy_ram_22).
wetland_management__asset_threat__drough.conditionality: Two of the four units are measurements — subsidence in Sumatra and bird numbers in a Belarus project evaluation; the other two are interpretation: the Hooijer authors' reading of their own record, and an expert statement with no frequency, site or measurement, made where the guidance itself notes there is very little literature on what happens after planting. The Belarus case is floodplain meadow kept open by grazing and mowing, a different wetland type and practice from tropical peat rewetting, and its indicator is birds rather than any livelihood; the evaluation also names drought and snowless winters as arriving faster and more severely than the project was designed for. Settings are upper-middle-income Indonesia and Belarus plus guidance with no site; there is no low-income or lower-middle-income case. Design implication: a wetland investment in a drought-prone setting should budget and monitor for drought-year losses of peat surface, carbon, plantings and habitat function rather than treat them as failure of the works, and should expect the asset to deliver least in the dry years.

wetland_management__asset_threat__drough.mechanism: Drought damages the restored wetland by taking away the water it runs on. In a rewetted Indonesian peat restoration area, peat-surface subsidence accelerated sharply during and shortly after the 2019 El Niño drought when groundwater depths were very low, running 2.5 to 4 times the rate of the preceding 3.5 years and more than double the 7.5-year mean (ev_climate_shock_hooi24_5). The authors read their long record as showing that a severe drought could still cause major water-table drops to near 1 m below the peat surface, with carbon-emission spikes, even in otherwise rewetted conditions, in restoration areas and remaining peat-swamp forest alike (ev_climate_shock_hooi24_6). On a restored floodplain the hazard works by removing the flood the wetland depends on: in 2020, lack of snow cover and severe drought meant no spring flooding on the Pripyat floodplain, and migrating and nesting birds on the restored floodplain meadows declined strongly (ev_wgy_blr_6).
wetland_management__asset_threat__drough.conditionality: One unit in each source is a measurement — subsidence in Sumatra, bird numbers in a Belarus project evaluation; the second Indonesian unit is the authors' reading of their own record rather than an independent measurement. The two cases are different wetland types and practices: canal-blocking rewetting of a retired pulpwood plantation on tropical peat, and floodplain meadows kept open by grazing and mowing on a temperate river, with birds rather than any livelihood as the indicator. The Belarus evaluation also names drought and snowless winters as arriving faster and more severely than the project was designed for. Both settings are upper-middle-income; the scope is in context for those, and nothing here was measured in a low-income or lower-middle-income country. Design implication: budget and monitor for drought-year losses of peat surface, carbon and habitat function rather than treat them as failure of the works, and expect the asset to deliver least in the dry years.

wetland_management__asset_threat__extrem.mechanism: The vulnerable asset is the canal dam that holds the water table up. In December 2005, after an extreme rainfall event, both dams in the Kalampangan Canal were damaged by water seeping underneath and along the sides; they were repaired in March 2006 and were damaged again in August 2006 (ev_climate_shock_ritz13_7). During an extreme rainfall event in August 2007 a further dam was damaged in a flash flood, the canal water level rising by several metres in a short period (ev_climate_shock_ritz13_8). The rainfall is the trigger; the vulnerability is structural, since highly permeable tropical peat lets seepage pass beneath and alongside a dam, and the sunken canals intercept overland and interflow, raising canal discharges when the rain is extreme.
wetland_management__asset_threat__extrem.conditionality: This is a single demonstration site in Indonesian tropical peat, recorded as a case study rather than measured across projects, and the repeat failure after repair is the most transferable part of it. It says nothing about damage to the wetland itself, about coastal or temperate wetland types, or about water-control structures of other designs. Read it as a design and maintenance risk for canal-blocking programmes in deep permeable peat — dam siting relative to the contour, seepage control, and a repair budget that assumes recurrence — rather than as a general sensitivity of wetland management to extreme rainfall. Provenance: humid-tropical, upper-middle-income, with no comparable record from any other peat region.

wetland_management__asset_threat__fire.mechanism: Fire can destroy restoration work, especially new plantings, before it establishes. Ramsar guidance reports that many planted areas in degraded tropical peat swamp forest have been lost to fire [ev_wgy_ram_20]. In Central Kalimantan, project staff said fires had damaged the trees they planted and that recurring fires would destroy most of them [ev_climate_shock_pusp21_3]. In a Sumatran project, almost 50% of a restoration area burned in the 2019 El Nino [ev_wet_assetfire_budi20_1], and a review warns that recurrent fires on degraded peat put the restoration programme at high risk of failure [ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_8].
wetland_management__asset_threat__fire.conditionality: No source measures how much is lost, so the damage is not sized. The evidence is expert statements, interviews and a single project site, all from Indonesian peatland. It does not say whether the burned plantings were on rewetted or still-drained peat. Treat it as a reason to budget for fire protection and replanting, not as a loss rate.
wetland_management__asset_threat__fire.agreement_note: All four sources agree that fire damages restoration work.

wetland_management__asset_threat__flood.mechanism: Flooding can destroy restoration plantings and the structures that keep peat wet. The Ramsar technical guidance records, from its authors' knowledge, that a large number of planted areas in degraded tropical peat-swamp forest have been lost to flooding, as well as to fire, drought and out-competition by ferns and sedges (ev_wgy_ram_21). In South Sumatra, canal blockings were damaged due to flooding in the 2018 wet season, and in the 2019 prolonged dry season the damaged blockings and surrounding open canals lowered the water table in the project area (ev_wet_assetflood_budi20_1). A review of tropical peatland restoration techniques (Dohong et al. 2018) cites a study in Berbak National Park, Jambi, where prolonged and deep flooding in 2004 had killed most of the seedlings planted and the survival rate remained at 5% (van Eijk et al. 2009) [ev_climate_shock_doh18_1].
wetland_management__asset_threat__flood.conditionality: The Ramsar line is a single expert statement, with no site, frequency, area or measurement, made where the guidance notes there is very little literature on what happens after planting. It does not say whether the flooding came from rivers or from the raised water table of rewetting itself, and it concerns tropical peat-swamp replanting only. The Berbak figure is the only measured loss rate, reported second-hand from van Eijk et al. at a single national-park site [ev_climate_shock_doh18_1]. Together these are a reason to budget for replanting losses and replacement, not a measured rate of loss. The Sumatran case is a single site on a project its authors describe as never fully rewetted; the sentence is cut by a page break, so the number of damaged blockings is not recoverable. What it does show is the mechanism of loss - flood damage to the dams undoing the rewetting in the following dry season - which argues for budgeting dam inspection and repair after each wet season.

wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.mechanism: Wetland management strongly increases biodiversity. Putting water and vegetation back into a drained or damaged wetland restores the conditions wetland species need, and species return from nearby sources. A global meta-analysis found restoring degraded wetlands raised biodiversity by 19%, with clear gains for vertebrates, plants and invertebrates [ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_3]. Reopening tidal flow on coasts produced gains in 57% of monitoring studies [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_1]. Creating wetlands in farmland adds habitat the landscape has lost: in Sweden each new wetland added species to the regional total [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3], and lagoons built on Australian sugarcane farms held at least 36 native fish species [ev_wet_eff_cann22_1]. Rewetting drained German fens is expected to bring back fen plants and animals [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tann22_2], and in Indonesia a model found restoring lost peat swamp forest could remove the extinction risk for its forest birds [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tan22_3]. A Chinese coastal project that turned fish ponds back into a bird roost saw shorebird numbers rise markedly [ev_biodiversity_outcome_rgwo25_6].
wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.conditionality: The gains are measured against the damaged starting point; compared with intact wetlands, restored sites usually fall short, which is incomplete recovery, not harm [ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_1]. How restoration is done matters: peat sites left to recover on their own are modelled as stagnating or getting worse for decades [ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_6, ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_5]. Harms do occur: rewetting can destroy rare dry habitats that have developed on drained peat [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tann22_3], and a tidal project's most common fish was a non-native predator of the endangered fish it was meant to help [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_2]. Some groups, such as bottom-dwelling invertebrates, showed no change [ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_4, ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_7]. Few results give a size. The Chinese bird count is grey literature from a single site with no comparison, the Indonesian figure is modelled, and almost all measured evidence is from high- and upper-middle-income countries. A review also cites a North American case where restoring individual wetlands did not bring back the Topeka Shiner, a small fish, and the authors argue that species moving between wetlands need restoration across many wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_maxw26w1_3].

wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.mechanism: On tropical peat, rewetting removes the drainage that keeps the site degraded, and native trees can return without planting where seed can still arrive: native peat swamp forest trees were found growing on their own, at high density, in the wettest parts of a Sumatran restoration area [ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3]. Restoring forest cover on degraded peat is expected to bring back biodiversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4], and a model of Indonesian peatlands found that restoring the swamp forest lost since 2000 could cut the extinction risk of its forest birds from 14% to 0% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tan22_3].
wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.conditionality: The gain is real in direction but not sized. The Sumatran plots all lay close to remaining forest, a best case for seed arrival, and the regrowth cannot be credited to rewetting alone [ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3]. The forest-cover statement is an expected benefit, and the bird result is a model that assumes restoration happens at once [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4, ev_biodiversity_outcome_tan22_3]. All evidence is from upper-middle-income Southeast Asia, none from farmed or low-income landscapes. Check distance to remaining forest first, and plan local monitoring.
wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.agreement_note: All sources point to gains, but none gives a measured size.

wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.mechanism: In cropping landscapes, the gain comes from adding water habitat where little remains. Creating wetlands across Swedish farm catchments raised landscape biodiversity, particularly where the density of water habitats rose by at least 30%, and each new wetland added species to the regional total [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3]. In Ohio, a planted wetland basin stayed richer in plants for 10 years than an unplanted one [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7]. Lagoons built on Australian sugarcane farms held at least 36 native fish species [ev_wet_eff_cann22_1].
wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.conditionality: No size is given for the gain at a single site; the Swedish gain builds up across many wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3]. The Swedish wetlands were built mainly to trap nutrients, the Ohio comparison is planting against no planting, and the Australian lagoons had no before survey [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7, ev_wet_eff_cann22_1]. All evidence is from temperate or high-income farmland; nothing is from tropical or low-income rainfed systems.

wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.mechanism: In high-income settings the gain is moderate and comes from adding or re-making wetland habitat in landscapes that have lost it, and from active work on the site. In Sweden each new farmland wetland added species to the regional total, still rising after many wetlands were built [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3]. Lagoons built on Australian sugarcane farms held at least 36 native fish species [ev_wet_eff_cann22_1]. A review of German fens concludes that rewetting drained fens will increase fen plants and animals [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tann22_2]. Reopening tidal flow gave biodiversity gains in 57% of monitoring studies [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_1], and a Danube floodplain project in Bulgaria saw fish and bird numbers rise quickly after the first flooding [ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_2].
wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.conditionality: The class is moderate because few results give a size. Doing too little can fail: passively restored peat is modelled as stagnating or getting worse for decades [ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_6]. Rewetting can harm rare dry habitats that have developed on drained peat, a conflict between climate and nature goals [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tann22_3]. A tidal project's most common fish was a non-native predator of the endangered fish it aimed to help [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_2]. Some groups did not change [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_7]. Swedish created wetlands came close to, but did not quite match, mature reference ponds for regional diversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_5]. The Australian lagoons had no before survey, and the Bulgarian figures are early project reports. All evidence here is from Europe, North America and Australia. A review also cites a North American case where restoring individual wetlands did not bring back the Topeka Shiner, a small fish, and the authors argue that species moving between wetlands need restoration across many wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_maxw26w1_3].

wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.mechanism: The only low- and lower-middle-income evidence describes wetlands that provide habitat where water is put back on the land. In the Amu Darya delta of Uzbekistan, wetlands formed on drainage collectors are reported, on anecdotal evidence from site visits and State Committee reports, to present adequate living conditions for fauna and flora and an adequate substitute for the drained eastern part of Lake Ayaskala [ev_biodiversity_outcome_uzicr_2].
wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.conditionality: Neither unit measures a change caused by the practice. The Uzbek claim is an evaluator's assertion resting on anecdote, and the wetlands it describes are a by-product of a bundled drainage-rerouting and irrigation programme in an irrigated cropping landscape [ev_biodiversity_outcome_uzicr_2]. The Ugandan Green Climate Fund evaluation is a baseline report: wetland systems showed few significant differences in phytoplankton, green algae, flagellates, zooplankton and crustaceans between treatment and comparison sites, which describes conditions at the start of a restoration bundled with access restrictions and alternative livelihood support, not its effect [ev_biodiversity_outcome_fp034b_1]. No unit gives a magnitude, and no unit measures vertebrates, plants or species of conservation concern in a low-income farmed landscape.

wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.mechanism: In upper-middle-income settings, rewetting and replanting let wetland species return. A meta-analysis of China's coastal wetland restoration found biodiversity 36.8% higher in restored than in degraded wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_1]. Native peat swamp trees regrew on their own in the wettest parts of a Sumatran site [ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3], and a model of Indonesian peatlands found that restoring lost swamp forest could cut the extinction risk of its forest birds from 14% to 0% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tan22_3]. Rewetting a cut-over peatland in Belarus brought reed and sedge back over a large area [ev_wgy_blr_7], and on the Chinese coast a project that turned fish ponds into a bird roost saw shorebird numbers rise markedly [ev_biodiversity_outcome_rgwo25_6].
wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.conditionality: Only the Chinese meta-analysis gives a measured size, and it also shows restored sites still 10.7% below reference wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_1]. The Sumatran case is a best case near remaining forest [ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3], the Indonesian bird result is modelled, and the Chinese roost count is grey literature from a single site with no comparison, where a wider wetland park was set up at the same time [ev_biodiversity_outcome_rgwo25_6]. The Belarus area fell short of its own target [ev_wgy_blr_7]. None of this is from farmed landscapes or lower-income countries; local monitoring should go with any investment.
wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.agreement_note: All sources point to gains; none reports harm.

wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.mechanism: Wetland management moderately increases carbon storage. Raising the water table on drained peat stops the stored carbon from rotting away, so carbon dioxide losses fall, even though methane rises. Rewetting drained farmland peat in Germany is estimated to save 20 to 35 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per hectare a year [ev_wet_carbon_meye26_1], and each 10 cm the water table is raised cuts net warming by at least 3 tonnes per hectare a year [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_1]. IPCC guidance adds that rewetting cuts waterborne carbon losses (a median 36% in the studies it collated) and that nitrous oxide falls practically to zero once the water table is within 20 cm of the surface [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc13wl_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc13wl_3]. Restored forested wetlands on former US farmland were modelled to store 15.8 to 92.4 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per hectare every five years [ev_carbon_sequestration_jenk10_1], and in Canada active moss reintroduction restored carbon uptake on extracted peat [ev_carbon_sequestration_unepgpa22_2]. Field studies confirm that blocking ditches and canals raises the water table [ev_water_table_depth_hold04_1, ev_water_table_depth_page09_1, ev_water_table_depth_wils11db_1]. On burned peat in South Sumatra, planted native trees took up 11.3 tonnes of CO2 per hectare a year (Shorea balangeran) and 12.4 tonnes (Dyera polyphylla) in their wood [ev_wet_carbon_budi20_1, ev_wet_carbon_budi20_2]. Reviews of Indonesian peat projects report canal blocks raising the water table: by about 60 cm in the dry season 100 m from a block in Riau, by 70 cm within 170 m of a block at Sungai Tohor, and by a metre over 2420 ha where communities built 12 blocks [ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_2, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_4, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_3].
wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.conditionality: The class is moderate because the size rests on modelled results. Methane is the trade-off: where water stands above the peat surface, methane warming can outweigh the carbon dioxide saved for years [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_4], and restored wetlands can warm the climate for their first years to decades, with the switch to net cooling estimated at 57 to 299 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_4]. A meta-analysis found methane up 122.3% after restoration, with total emissions no higher than before [ev_carbon_sequestration_xu25_3]. Partial rewetting slows but does not stop peat loss [ev_carbon_sequestration_unepgpa22_4]. In a Kalimantan simulation, raising water levels gave only a small, not significant fall in carbon dioxide [ev_carbon_sequestration_page09_2], and planting on rewetted tropical peat has failed: seedlings did no better beside a dammed canal, and aerial seeding survived at about 2% [ev_establishment_survival_page09_6, ev_establishment_survival_pusp21_4]. Most evidence is temperate, boreal and high-income, and the benefit goes to the climate, not to the farmer. The South Sumatra tree figures count carbon in the trees only, not the peat below, and come from a single project; the Indonesian water-table results are cited second-hand in a review [ev_wet_carbon_budi20_1, ev_wet_carbon_budi20_2, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_2].

wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.mechanism: In the humid tropics, rewetting drained peat slows subsidence and the peat decay behind it [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_1], and canal blocking in Kalimantan raised the dry-season water table [ev_water_table_depth_page09_1]. A planning model for Indonesian peatlands counts large avoided emissions from restoration, mostly from preventing peat decay and fire [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan22_2]. On the methane side, measured fluxes after damming in Kalimantan moved in opposite directions at paired sites [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_4].
wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.conditionality: There is not enough evidence to set a class. Almost every unit here reports a single gas or subsidence alone, with no net balance of carbon dioxide against methane; the only net figure is from a single modelled source that assumes immediate restoration [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan22_2]. In a Kalimantan simulation, raising water levels gave only a small, not significant fall in carbon dioxide [ev_carbon_sequestration_page09_2]. Revegetation is also unreliable: seedlings did no better beside a dammed canal, and aerial seeding survived at about 2% [ev_establishment_survival_page09_6, ev_establishment_survival_pusp21_4]. A measured net greenhouse-gas balance from a rewetted tropical site would let this row state a class.

wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.mechanism: Raising the water table on drained peat stops the stored carbon from rotting away, so carbon dioxide losses fall even though methane rises. Rewetting drained farmland peat in Germany is estimated to save 20 to 35 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per hectare a year [ev_wet_carbon_meye26_1]; a German scenario of wet farming on fen peat cut emissions in a single state from 5.5 to 1.2 to 3.1 million tonnes a year [ev_carbon_sequestration_tann22_1]; and each 10 cm the water table is raised cuts net warming by at least 3 tonnes per hectare a year [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_1]. Restored forested wetlands on US farmland were modelled to store 15.8 to 92.4 tonnes per hectare every five years [ev_carbon_sequestration_jenk10_1], and in Canada moss reintroduction restored carbon uptake on extracted peat [ev_carbon_sequestration_unepgpa22_2]. Ditch and drain blocking on UK bogs raised the water table in dry periods [ev_water_table_depth_hold04_1, ev_water_table_depth_wils11db_1].
wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.conditionality: The class is moderate because the size rests on modelled results. Methane is the trade-off: where water stands above the peat surface, methane warming can outweigh the carbon dioxide saved for years [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_4]; on forestry-drained peat, methane can cancel all of the cooling for decades [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_5]; and restored wetlands can warm the climate for their first years to decades, with the switch to net cooling estimated at 57 to 299 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_4]. The Canadian figure is a second-hand report that leaves out the carbon in the extracted peat [ev_carbon_sequestration_unepgpa22_2]. The Welsh water-table rise was slight [ev_water_table_depth_wils11db_1]. All evidence is from high-income temperate and boreal countries, and the benefit goes to the climate, not to the farmer.
wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.agreement_note: Most sources show net carbon gains; three show warming over some period, mostly from methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_1].

wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.mechanism: The only result here that weighs all gases together found no difference: a global meta-analysis found methane rose by 122.3% after restoration, yet total greenhouse-gas emissions of restored wetlands were no higher than those of disturbed wetlands, because carbon dioxide fell [ev_carbon_sequestration_xu25_3]. IPCC guidance adds that rewetting cuts waterborne carbon losses (a median 36% across collated studies) and that nitrous oxide falls practically to zero when the water table is within 20 cm of the surface [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc13wl_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc13wl_3]. The UN peatland assessment says partly raising water levels gives some climate benefit [ev_carbon_sequestration_unepgpa22_4], and a meta-analysis found soil carbon 13.8% higher in restored than in cultivated wetlands [ev_soil_organic_carbon_xu19_1].
wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.conditionality: The no-effect class is weak: it means restored wetlands did not emit more than disturbed ones, not that restoration does nothing for the climate [ev_carbon_sequestration_xu25_3]. Most other units cover a single gas or carbon pool and cannot set a direction. Methane rises mainly where the water table rises [ev_carbon_sequestration_xu25_7]. Partial rewetting slows peat loss but does not stop it [ev_carbon_sequestration_unepgpa22_4]. Soil carbon fell after restoration in some warm, wet or tidal settings [ev_soil_organic_carbon_xu19_3]. The sources pool many countries and restoration types; read this row alongside the peatland and rewetting rows, which carry net balances.
wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.agreement_note: Sources split between gains on single gases or pools and a net result of no difference [ev_carbon_sequestration_xu25_3].

wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.mechanism: In upper-middle-income peatlands, mostly Indonesia and Malaysia, the evidence points to a carbon benefit of unstated size: rewetting slows subsidence and the peat decay behind it, and carbon dioxide from peat is lowest when the water table is near the surface [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_jauhiainen16_1]. Canal blocking in Kalimantan raised the dry-season water table [ev_water_table_depth_page09_1]. A planning model for Indonesian peatlands counts large avoided emissions from restoration, mostly from preventing peat decay and fire [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan22_2], and a synthesis judges rewetting a better climate option than keeping peat drained [ev_carbon_sequestration_lup23_1]. On burned peat in South Sumatra, planted native trees took up 11.3 tonnes of CO2 per hectare a year (Shorea balangeran) and 12.4 tonnes (Dyera polyphylla) in their wood [ev_wet_carbon_budi20_1, ev_wet_carbon_budi20_2]. Reviews of Indonesian peat projects report canal blocks raising the water table: by about 60 cm in the dry season 100 m from a block in Riau, by 70 cm within 170 m of a block at Sungai Tohor, and by a metre over 2420 ha where communities built 12 blocks [ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_2, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_4, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_3].
wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.conditionality: The size is not stated because almost no unit weighs carbon dioxide against methane: most report a single gas, subsidence or national totals. In a Kalimantan simulation, raising water levels gave only a small, not significant fall in carbon dioxide [ev_carbon_sequestration_page09_2]; laboratory work suggests peat keeps decaying even when waterlogged [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauhiainen16_2]; and methane moved in opposite directions at paired sites [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_4]. The planning model assumes immediate restoration. Revegetation is unreliable: seedlings did no better beside a dammed canal, and aerial seeding survived at about 2% [ev_establishment_survival_page09_6, ev_establishment_survival_pusp21_4]. A measured net balance from a rewetted site in this income group would strengthen the row. The South Sumatra tree figures count carbon in the trees only, not the peat below, and come from a single project; the Indonesian water-table results are cited second-hand in a review [ev_wet_carbon_budi20_1, ev_wet_carbon_budi20_2, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_2].

wetland_management__catchment_water_yiel.mechanism: Blocking ditches in drained peatland raises the water table close to the ditch: across boreal and temperate wetlands, restoration raised groundwater by 22 cm near the work, about as much as drainage had lowered it [ev_wetflA_bring_gw_rise, ev_wetflA_bring_conclusion]. After drains were blocked on a Welsh bog, stream flows stayed higher and fell away more slowly during dry spells [ev_water_yield_wils11db_2]. In a Canadian basin model, adding wetland area gradually offset the fall in summer low flows expected under climate change [ev_wet_eff_goy22_2].
wetland_management__catchment_water_yiel.conditionality: The size is not stated and the gain is local: the groundwater rise fell to 50% within about 9 m of the ditch, and effects beyond the wetland could not be judged [ev_wetflA_bring_gw_decay, ev_wetflA_bring_outside_inconclusive]. Average flows from the same Welsh site fell after blocking, mainly because less time was spent at peak flow [ev_water_yield_wils11db_3]. In the Canadian model, a restoration scenario made summer low flows worse in some sub-catchments [ev_wet_eff_goy22_3]. All evidence is from high-income, temperate or boreal settings, partly modelled, and none measures water reaching farmers downstream.
wetland_management__catchment_water_yiel.agreement_note: Most results show more water held or released in dry periods; two sources show lower flows in some settings [ev_wet_eff_goy22_3, ev_water_yield_wils11db_3].

wetland_management__coastal__asset_threa.mechanism: Storms wear down and tear coastal wetlands, but the damage is rated low. A review of storm impacts on coastal wetland elevations records that in 2002 Hurricane Lili created 257 ha of open water, 0.5-1.3 m deep, at West Cote Blanche, Louisiana, by moving the marsh root mat sideways [ev_climate_shock_cah06_2], and that Hurricane Andrew compacted a severely degraded marsh at Bayou Chitigue by 33 mm in spite of sediment deposition [ev_climate_shock_cah06_3]. A second review, citing a global analysis of salt-marsh erosion and wave measurements, finds that most salt-marsh wear is caused by moderate storms that come about monthly [ev_erosion_hazard_leon17_6], while intense hurricanes contribute less than 1% to long-term salt-marsh erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_leon17_5].
wetland_management__coastal__asset_threa.conditionality: The condition of the wetland decides how much damage is done. A healthy marsh nearby at Old Oyster Bayou was not compacted by Hurricane Andrew but instead gained height equal to the sediment laid down [ev_climate_shock_cah06_4], against the compaction of the degraded marsh [ev_climate_shock_cah06_3], so a newly planted or degraded site, where the ground is weakest, is the case to budget for. All the measurements are on existing, established marsh on US coasts, not on restored or created sites [ev_climate_shock_cah06_2], and the erosion analysis is cited second-hand and covers only erosion of the marsh edge [ev_erosion_hazard_leon17_5]. A small share of long-term erosion is not a damage rate per storm: it is compatible with heavy losses in the year a hurricane arrives, and edge retreat under ordinary monthly storms is a continuing upkeep cost [ev_erosion_hazard_leon17_6].

wetland_management__coastal__biodiversit.mechanism: Replanting marsh or reopening tidal flow rebuilds the habitat and flooding pattern coastal species need. A meta-analysis of China's coastal restoration found biodiversity 36.8% higher in restored than in degraded wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_1]. Reopening tidal flow gave gains in most monitoring studies, with commercially important fish among those responding [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_3]. Protection of lagoons in Ghana coincided with a large rise in wading birds [ev_biodiversity_outcome_ghicr_1], and a Chinese project that turned fish ponds into a high-tide roost saw shorebird numbers rise markedly [ev_biodiversity_outcome_rgwo25_6].
wetland_management__coastal__biodiversit.conditionality: Restored marshes still had fewer plant species than natural marshes, and biodiversity overall was 10.7% below reference sites [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_13, ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_2]. Bottom-dwelling invertebrates showed little change [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_7]. A tidal project's most common fish was a non-native predator of the endangered native fish it aimed to help [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_2]. The tidal review warns its scoring may overstate positive results [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_1]. The Ghana units describe protecting existing lagoons, not restoring them, and the evaluation says the lagoons remain under threat [ev_biodiversity_outcome_ghppar_1]. The Chinese roost result is grey literature from a single site with no comparison. Most evidence is from China and the United States.
wetland_management__coastal__biodiversit.agreement_note: Most sources report gains; one reports harm from an invasive fish [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_2], and some groups show no change [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_7].

wetland_management__coastal__carbon_sequ.mechanism: Coastal wetlands (mangroves and salt marshes) are strong natural carbon sinks because they take up far more carbon dioxide than the methane they emit. A comparison of wetland types found mangroves and salt marshes were the only two that remained net carbon sinks, because of the limited methane generated in coastal wetlands compared with the scale of carbon-dioxide uptake [ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_5]. A global meta-analysis of natural coastal wetlands found that converting them to other land uses increased their greenhouse-gas warming potential by 7.8 times for constructed wetlands, 22.3 times for cropland and 29.5 times for aquaculture ponds on average, implying a correspondingly large potential benefit from protecting or restoring the wetland instead of converting it [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan20_1].
wetland_management__coastal__carbon_sequ.conditionality: This class is built from a very small, specific evidence base, just two sources, both studying existing or converted coastal wetlands rather than restoration projects measured directly, so the strong_positive rating does not mean every restoration project will show this scale of gain. Other meta-analyses of the same coastal systems find a much more mixed picture: a global meta-analysis found no significant difference in carbon-dioxide or nitrous-oxide flux between restored and natural salt marshes, though restored marshes had significantly lower methane flux than natural ones [ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_11, ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_12]; the same study found restored and natural marshes accumulated soil carbon at statistically indistinguishable rates, even though restored marshes' total carbon stocks still lagged behind natural marshes [ev_soil_organic_carbon_liu24_10]; and a separate meta-analysis found restored coastal wetlands showed no significant improvement in soil organic carbon compared with degraded wetlands, while restored inland wetlands did show a significant gain [ev_soil_organic_carbon_wu25w1_5]. A global meta-analysis of restored wetlands found soil organic carbon was significantly lower than in cultivated and natural wetlands specifically where restoration used a plantation approach, where the wetland had tidal hydrology after restoration, or in wetter, warmer or lower-latitude sites [ev_soil_organic_carbon_xu19_5]. Establishment itself is also a gamble: across a large pooled dataset the mean survival rate of coastal wetland plantings was only 53%, with 17% of observations seeing more than 95% of transplants survive and 23% seeing less than 5% survive [ev_establishment_survival_liu24_1, ev_establishment_survival_liu24_2]. The underlying studies are concentrated in China, North America and other high-income or upper-middle-income settings; applying this class to low- and middle-income rural coastal contexts is a transfer outside where the evidence was measured.

wetland_management__coastal__cost_per_he.mechanism: Every unit in this row comes from the same global salt-marsh review, which reports project budgets divided by the area restored. Mean total cost per hectare at unprotected sites is USD 495,067-876,564 in middle-income countries [ev_project_cost_wang22_1] and USD 454,285-694,724 in high-income countries [ev_project_cost_wang22_2]. Broken out by method, within the middle-income unprotected cell, hydrological restoration costs USD 6,090-9,945 per hectare [ev_project_cost_wang22_3] while vegetation restoration costs USD 26,945-42,756 [ev_project_cost_wang22_4]. What a coastal project does therefore drives its cost far more than where it is done.
wetland_management__coastal__cost_per_he.conditionality: A single source carries the whole row, so there is no cross-source check on it. The headline per-hectare totals are flagged by the compilers as implausibly high for a landscape intervention: project areas are small and the budgets include engineering, hard structures and land, so the ordinal reading (coastal restoration is expensive, and hydrological work is its cheapest component) is what transfers, not the number. The quoted ranges are the spread across the review's alternative monetary conversion methods, not confidence intervals. The evidence base is China, Great Britain, the Netherlands and the United States; it is not a low- or lower-middle-income cost, and tidal and marsh engineering costs should not be carried to inland or smallholder settings.

wetland_management__coastal__cost_reduct.mechanism: Both units come from the same global tidal-reinstatement review and both describe cost rising, not falling. Tidal reinstatement is often more cost-intensive than other types of coastal wetland restoration because it requires hydrological engineering, land acquisition, feasibility assessments, spatial modelling and complex regulatory compliance and permits [ev_project_cost_tidal26_5]. Reported project costs vary widely with scale and setting: Colombia's Ciénaga Grande de Santa Marta at 128,000 ha cost US$20.1 million, against US$1.17 million for the 38 ha Galilee Saltmarsh Restoration in the United States [ev_project_cost_tidal26_4].
wetland_management__coastal__cost_reduct.conditionality: A single source carries the row, and it reports project totals with no comparable per-hectare denominator, so the two schemes cannot be put on the same scale without arithmetic the source does not perform. Nothing here measures avoided or reduced cost, so the target name overstates what the pool contains. The reviewed projects are concentrated in the United States, Australia and England, with Colombia the sole upper-middle-income case, and the review's own emphasis is that government funding is what carries the upfront cost — a condition that cannot be assumed in a low- or lower-middle-income investment. No class is stated: what is missing is a second independent source or one measured comparison of what a coastal wetland project saved against the alternative it replaced.

wetland_management__coastal__establishme.mechanism: The row rests on a single global meta-analysis figure: saltmarsh restoration was associated with the highest average total project costs among the wetland types compared, a median of US$89 660 per hectare per year of the restoration event, in 2010 US$ [ev_project_cost_tail20w1_6]. The figure covers whole projects, including the hydrological manipulation that marsh restoration may require.
wetland_management__coastal__establishme.conditionality: The Taillardat per-hectare-per-year figures are TOTAL PROJECT costs, the capital of the restoration event annualised over its duration, not maintenance; that is why they sit in establishment cost and not recurrent cost (the cost-routing rule), and they must not be read as a yearly running bill. They are 2010 US$ medians over actual and planned projects. The saltmarsh projects behind the median were all in high-income countries, and a single source carries the row, so there is no cross-source check. It orients on scale only; no low- or middle-income coastal establishment cost is in this row [ev_project_cost_tail20w1_6].

wetland_management__coastal__flood__all.mechanism: Coastal wetlands (salt marshes, mangroves) reduce flood impact mainly by dissipating wave energy and attenuating storm surge before it reaches land: salt-marsh vegetation has been measured giving a significant reduction in wave height compared with unvegetated mudflat, and across a global set of field measurements, coastal habitats reduced wave heights by 35% to 71% on average, with salt marshes alone cutting wave height by about 72%. Croplands within 1 km of mangroves and tidal marshes have also been found to experience less surface-water presence and smaller crop-cover declines than more distant areas.
wetland_management__coastal__flood__all.conditionality: This benefit does not hold at every severity level: the same review found salt marshes dissipate storm surge less effectively during extreme storms than during moderate ones, man-made levees and dikes behind a marsh can limit its surge-attenuating effect, and one study found neither crop type nor the simple presence of coastal wetlands added much explanatory power once other factors were accounted for. Only 2 of the 8 units measuring a benefit actually state its size, which is why the class is capped at a moderate level even though the direction is consistent. For most farmers this is an off-site benefit: the wetland sits off their land, and the protection shows up downstream or at landscape scale, not on their own plot.
wetland_management__coastal__flood__all.agreement_note: A sizeable share of the pooled units found no measurable benefit, or an attenuation effect that breaks down under the most extreme storms, which is why the class is capped rather than rated strong despite high agreement on the overall direction.

wetland_management__coastal__flood_hazar.mechanism: Coastal wetlands reduce flood hazard mainly by dissipating wave energy and attenuating storm surge before it reaches land: salt-marsh vegetation has been measured giving significantly greater wave attenuation than unvegetated intertidal mudflat, and across a global set of field measurements, coastal habitats reduced wave heights by 35% to 71% on average, with salt marshes alone cutting wave height by about 72%. A sizeable proportion of salt-marsh and mangrove restoration projects report improved protection from storm events as an outcome.
wetland_management__coastal__flood_hazar.conditionality: The benefit is not uniform across storm severity: the same review found salt marshes attenuate storm surge less effectively during extreme storms than during moderate ones, and man-made levees or dikes behind a marsh can limit its surge-attenuating effect. Only 2 of the 8 units measuring a benefit state its size, which is why the class is capped at a moderate level even though the direction is consistent.

wetland_management__coastal__production_.mechanism: The only evidence is an association on the Queensland coast: after a cyclone, croplands within 1 km of mangroves and tidal marshes experienced reduced crop cover declines compared with more distant areas [ev_crop_yield_rowl26w1_2].
wetland_management__coastal__production_.conditionality: Neither unit may set a class. Both describe existing mangrove and tidal marsh, which the authors could not separate, not a restored or managed wetland, and the outcome is crop cover read from a satellite vegetation index, not yield or production. The binary presence of a coastal wetland on the seaward side of a field did not contribute substantially to the models [ev_crop_yield_rowl26w1_3], and the authors say the results do not provide direct evidence of causal protection. It is a single high-income Australian study in which only two crop types, irrigated sugarcane and mango, were present, so nothing here speaks to rainfed smallholder production gaps. No class is stated: what is missing is a measured production outcome on farmland beside a restored or created coastal wetland, compared with farmland without one.

wetland_management__coastal__recurrent_c.mechanism: Saltmarsh restoration was associated with the highest average total project costs in a global meta-analysis of wetland restoration costs, a median of US$89 660 per hectare per year of the restoration event, in 2010 US$ [ev_project_cost_tail20w1_6].
wetland_management__coastal__recurrent_c.conditionality: Those Taillardat medians are not running costs: they are total project costs spread over the duration of the restoration event, with one-off events counted as a single year, so they belong with establishment cost and must not be read as a yearly maintenance bill. They are 2010 US dollar medians over actual and planned projects. The saltmarsh projects behind the median were all in high-income countries, and the figure covers whole projects - including the hydrological manipulation that marsh restoration may require - divided over small restored areas. It orients on scale only; no low- or middle-income coastal cost is in this row.

wetland_management__coastal__rural_pover.mechanism: This row is about coastal protection economics and a single tourism case. Salt-marsh defences range from about as expensive as a breakwater to around three times cheaper, and about 40% of salt-marsh projects recover their cost within 30 years [ev_economic_return_nara16_6, ev_economic_return_wang22_5]. In China, turning fish ponds into a bird roost brought ecotourism income 10 times that of the previous fishery [ev_economic_return_rgwo25_7].
wetland_management__coastal__rural_pover.conditionality: There is not enough evidence to set a class. Most units measure value to society, such as avoided storm damage and engineering cost, not household income [ev_economic_return_nara16_3, ev_economic_return_wang22_5]. Marsh defences are not always cost effective [ev_economic_return_nara16_5]. The Chinese tourism figure is grey literature from a single project and does not say who received the income [ev_economic_return_rgwo25_7]. A measured household income result from a coastal wetland project is needed.

wetland_management__coastal__soil_erosio.mechanism: Marsh vegetation attenuates waves and currents as water passes through the canopy, so suspended sediment settles, the bed accretes and surface elevation is maintained while lateral erosion of the shoreline is reduced. That mechanism is measured from both ends: inside existing marsh against adjacent unvegetated mudflat, where most paired studies reported increased accretion or surface elevation or reduced erosion and the pooled effect on shoreline stabilisation was positive (ev_erosion_hazard_shep11_3, ev_erosion_hazard_shep11_4); and in planted marsh, which improved shoreline protection against degraded wetland (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_3). A meta-analysis of China's coastal wetland restoration (Liu et al.) found coastal stabilization - indicators such as vertical accretion rate - significantly improved in restored against degraded wetlands, by 19.7 % (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_1). A field experiment on a wave-stressed shoreline tests the mechanism from the loss side: lateral erosion where aboveground and belowground vegetation was removed (114.19 cm) was significantly higher than in vegetated controls (76.76 cm), whereas removing only the aboveground vegetation made no difference (ev_erosion_hazard_sill19w1_1, ev_erosion_hazard_sill19w1_2); across 15 previous comparisons of marsh-edge erosion between vegetated and vegetation-reduced conditions, the mean effect size of 1.22 shows a generally positive effect of vegetation on the reduction of marsh-edge erosion (ev_erosion_hazard_sill19w1_4).
wetland_management__coastal__soil_erosio.conditionality: Much of the pool is not a restoration result at all: the paired-study evidence measures what EXISTING marsh does against bare mudflat (ev_erosion_hazard_shep11_3, ev_erosion_hazard_shep11_4), which is an argument for protecting marsh that is already there rather than a measured gain from creating or replanting it, and a sizeable minority of those paired studies did not report a positive effect. The vegetation-removal experiment and its meta-analysis are the same kind of evidence - what existing marsh loses when its plants go, not what restoration adds - and vegetation had no effect on vertical erosion of the marsh surface (ev_erosion_hazard_sill19w1_3); their outcome is erosion of the marsh edge itself. The restored-versus-degraded pooled values are effect sizes and shares of studies whose scale the sources do not define (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_3), which is why direction is firmer than magnitude here; the Chinese stabilization figure pools restoration types that include building dikes as well as planting (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_1). This is shoreline and tidal-flat erosion only - it carries nothing about soil loss from cropland or rangeland - and the field sites are coasts in the United States, United Kingdom, China and the Netherlands, with the authors noting that matched restored and degraded pairs are few.

wetland_management__coastal__water_quali.mechanism: A restored coastal wetland slows tidal flow and waves, so suspended particles and the nutrients and contaminants bound to them drop out of the water column and are held in the marsh. A meta-analysis of China's coastal wetland restoration (Liu et al.) found water purification and waste treatment indicators significantly improved in restored against degraded wetlands, by 69.3 % [ev_nutrient_removal_liu24_1]. A planting meta-analysis adds the sediment side: sediment trapping by planted marsh matched or bettered the adjacent natural marsh [ev_sediment_retention_liu24_15].
wetland_management__coastal__water_quali.conditionality: The class is strong but rests on a single source: the Chinese meta-analysis, whose figure is a pooled response ratio for a broad water-purification category across restoration types from planting mangroves to breaking dikes, not a measured nitrogen or phosphorus load [ev_nutrient_removal_liu24_1]. The salt-marsh sediment result compares planted marsh with adjacent natural wetland, so it says a planted marsh may trap sediment at least as well as an intact one, hedged by its authors, not what planting changed against the pre-restoration shore, and it does not set the class [ev_sediment_retention_liu24_15]. Everything here is from the Chinese coast and high-income planted marsh; nothing comes from a low- or lower-middle-income farmed catchment. A second independent source measuring a nutrient or contaminant outcome below a restored coastal wetland would firm this up.

wetland_management__coastal__water_stres.mechanism: Restoring the hydrology of a degraded coastal wetland - planting, freshwater input, or breaking dikes to restore tidal flow - is the most direct way to restore its water-regulating function. A meta-analysis of China's coastal wetland restoration (Liu et al.) found hydrological regulation, among the regulating services, 124.8 % higher in restored than in degraded wetlands, the fastest-recovering service it assessed [ev_water_regulation_liu24_1].
wetland_management__coastal__water_stres.conditionality: The class rests on a single source, and within it on a thin subgroup of the meta-analysis, so the size is not robust [ev_water_regulation_liu24_1]. The outcome is a hydrological-regulation indicator of the wetland itself, not water available to farmers or relief of water stress on surrounding land, and coastal water is often brackish. It is from the Chinese coast, upper-middle-income; a second independent source measuring water supply or groundwater for users near a restored coastal wetland would be needed before this transfers.

wetland_management__coastal__wind_cyclon.mechanism: Coastal wetland standing between a cyclone and exposed property reduces the damage done, measured as an elasticity across US Atlantic and Gulf coastal counties: a 1% loss of coastal wetlands is associated with a 0.6% increase in property damage (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_1). Valued at the margin, the median county's wetland is worth about $91,000 per km2 per year in storm protection, against an average of about $1.8 million and a range from less than $800 to $100 million per km2 (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_4), and a counterfactual on a single hurricane put the damage attributable to prior wetland loss at about $430 million (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_5). A farm-level observation points the same way: after a cyclone on the Queensland coast, croplands within 1 km of mangroves and tidal marshes showed reduced crop cover declines compared with more distant areas (ev_crop_yield_rowl26w1_2).
wetland_management__coastal__wind_cyclon.conditionality: Protection is proportionately smallest where the storm is strongest: the elasticity of property damage with respect to wetlands is 0.58 for a tropical storm and 0.35 for a category 3 to 5 hurricane (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_2, ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_3). Built defences substitute for it — the elasticity is 0.50 in states with stricter building codes against 0.81 where codes and enforcement are weaker (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_6). All of this is measured on existing wetland cover rather than on a restoration project, and the same authors warn that a replacement wetland may take decades to fully develop the functions of the wetland it replaces (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_7), so the measured value is not what a new project delivers. The Queensland result is crop cover read from a satellite vegetation index, not yield, around existing mangrove and marsh that the authors could not separate, and the binary presence of a coastal wetland on the seaward side of a field did not contribute substantially to the models (ev_crop_yield_rowl26w1_3). Provenance: a US panel study of high-income coastal counties and an Australian satellite study; the US outcome is damage to coastal property, a societal and asset-owner benefit rather than a rural livelihood one, the Australian outcome is crop cover on farmland, and nothing in the cell speaks to a low-income or lower-middle-income coast.

wetland_management__cost_per_hectare_res.mechanism: Cost per hectare depends on what has to be built. Re-establishing water flows is the cheaper end: Indonesia's canal-blocking programme is estimated at US$2,300/ha [ev_wgy_ram_19], Indonesian peat restoration studies give figures from US$1625/ha to US$1866/ha [ev_wet_cost_jali25_2, ev_wet_cost_jali25_3, ev_project_cost_alex26_1], and controlled flooding of Danube marshes in Bulgaria cost US$1,903/ha [ev_project_cost_bgieg_1]. Replanting burned Indonesian peat costs around 1100 USD/ha [ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_7], and US forested-wetland restoration runs about $680 to $900/ha [ev_project_cost_jenk10_3]. Engineered coastal projects cost far more [ev_project_cost_wang22_2].
wetland_management__cost_per_hectare_res.conditionality: No figure is from a low- or lower-middle-income country, so no cost class is given and these orient rather than transfer. Figures differ in what they include, many are planning estimates or models, and none states a price year [ev_wet_cost_jali25_2, ev_wgy_ram_19]. The US figure leaves out land [ev_project_cost_jenk10_3]. Replanting burned peat still does not guarantee success [ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_7]. Read the figures as a scale: rewetting in the low thousands of US dollars per hectare, engineered coastal work much higher.

wetland_management__cost_per_hectare_res.mechanism: In high-income settings cost depends on scale and engineering. The Bulgarian Danube floodplain project cost US$1,903/ha [ev_project_cost_bgieg_1]; US forested-wetland restoration runs about $680 to $900/ha without land [ev_project_cost_jenk10_3]; and coastal salt-marsh projects run to hundreds of thousands of dollars per hectare [ev_project_cost_wang22_2].
wetland_management__cost_per_hectare_res.conditionality: The range is very wide because the salt-marsh figure divides total project cost over small coastal sites. The US figure excludes the land, and the landowner also gives up farm income [ev_project_cost_jenk10_3]. No source gives a price year. Valid for high-income settings only.

wetland_management__cost_reduction.mechanism: Restoration costs are pushed up by engineering, land and regulation rather than brought down: tidal reinstatement is described as more cost-intensive than other coastal restoration because it needs hydrological engineering, land acquisition, feasibility work, spatial modelling and permits [ev_project_cost_tidal26_5]. Scale matters: Colombia's Ciénaga Grande de Santa Marta (128,000 ha) cost US$20.1 million, while a 38 ha US saltmarsh project cost US$1.17 million [ev_project_cost_tidal26_4]. For wet farming on rewetted peat, specialised harvesting equipment and adapted production raise investment cost and risk above the drained baseline [ev_wet_cost_neud26_3]; Sphagnum farming establishment, calculated from pilot cost data in 2011 and again in 2016, fell between the dates but stayed in the order of a hundred thousand euros per hectare of production field [ev_wgy_wich_7].
wetland_management__cost_reduction.conditionality: The evidence is almost entirely high-income (US, European and Australian projects); nothing here shows restoration lowering farm or project costs. The Sphagnum figures fall between the two dates but stay far above conventional land use, and they are for a high-input pilot. Do not read the absence of cost-reduction evidence as proof that low-cost community-based rewetting in low-income settings cannot be cheap; it is simply not in the pool.

wetland_management__creation__biodiversi.mechanism: Creating wetlands in farmland adds habitat that the landscape has lost. Swedish created wetlands supported diversity similar to natural ponds in the region, each new wetland added species to the regional total, and pollution-sensitive insects made up a larger share of species than in reference ponds [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_4]. In Ohio, a planted basin stayed richer in plants for 10 years than an unplanted one [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7]. Lagoons built on Australian sugarcane farms held at least 36 native fish species [ev_wet_eff_cann22_1], and in Uzbekistan wetlands formed on drainage channels are reported to support wildlife [ev_biodiversity_outcome_uzicr_2].
wetland_management__creation__biodiversi.conditionality: No size is given for the gain from building a wetland where there was none; the Swedish results compare created wetlands with natural ponds [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_2]. The Swedish wetlands were built mainly to trap nutrients, the Australian lagoons had no before survey, and the Uzbek statement is an evaluator's view based on site visits [ev_wet_eff_cann22_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_uzicr_2]. The measured evidence is temperate and high-income.

wetland_management__creation__carbon_seq.mechanism: Creating a wetland builds a new carbon store from scratch. In created riverine basins in Ohio, organic matter in surface soils increased by approximately 1% per 3-year period over the decade after construction [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mits05_6], and nitrous oxide fluxes from marsh and edge plots were lower when those plots were inundated than when the same plots were exposed to air [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_9]. Shallow lakes created on former peat-extraction sites had the potential to reduce net greenhouse-gas flux through carbon sequestration [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_8].
wetland_management__creation__carbon_seq.conditionality: The methane cost of putting water onto land sits in the same sources. Methane emission from vegetated areas rose significantly when flooding reached zones that previously had no standing water, although average emission from pulsed sites stayed below that of permanently flooded sites [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_8], and the created shallow lakes caused methane emissions to the atmosphere even as they offered a net flux reduction [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_9]. The nitrous oxide benefit reaches only as far as the water does: in the upland plots, fluxes did not differ between flooded and dry periods [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_10]. Because the register has no variable for an individual gas, the carbon dioxide and nitrous-oxide gains and the methane rise from the same experiment enter the pool with opposite signs, which makes the evidence look more divided than it is: both sources report a net gain with a methane penalty inside it. The row rests on a pair of pumped experimental basins in temperate Ohio and a review of boreal and northern European peat-extraction after-use. wetland_management__creation__flood__all.mechanism: There is not enough evidence to rate this. The only finding is a review of natural flood management, which reports that storage areas, both blocked drains and ponds set aside from the channel, reduce peak flow in field and model studies [ev_wetflA_zhu_storage_effective].
wetland_management__creation__flood__all.conditionality: This is a single review reporting other studies, from a rich country, with no size given [ev_wetflA_zhu_storage_effective]. The review says where storage is placed matters most. Nothing here covers extreme floods. A measured result from a created wetland, or a second independent source, is needed before a rating can be given.

wetland_management__creation__flood__cro.mechanism: Created storage holds back part of a storm before it reaches the river. A review of natural flood management finds that storage areas reduce peak flow in field and model studies [ev_wetflA_zhu_storage_effective]. wetland_management__creation__flood__cro.conditionality: The size of the benefit is not stated. Where storage is placed matters most [ev_wetflA_zhu_storage_effective]. The Queensland result comes from a package of drains and lagoons, not wetlands alone [ev_wet_eff_cann22_2]. Nothing here covers extreme floods. Both settings are high-income.
wetland_management__creation__flood__cro.agreement_note: Both sources point to less flooding.

wetland_management__creation__recurrent_.mechanism: Where wetlands are built on farmland, the standing cost in this US national model is the land payment that covers the opportunity cost of land removed from agricultural production: land rental costs for cropland are, in the mean, more than five times greater than those for pastureland, at US$274 ± 156 per hectare [ev_project_cost_cheng20_6]. Design, construction and maintenance enter the same framework as area-dependent costs, annualised over a 50-year management horizon at a real discount rate of 4%.
wetland_management__creation__recurrent_.conditionality: This is a modelled national cost framework for constructed nutrient-retention wetlands, and its recurrent item is a US cropland rental rate, which prices forgone agriculture in a high-income economy; it cannot be read across to a low- or lower-middle-income landscape, where the opportunity cost of farmland is set by quite different land and tenure arrangements. Keep the denominator per hectare per year, apart from establishment cost. The general point is structural: where a wetland is created on farmland, the standing cost is the production forgone, not the maintenance of the works.

wetland_management__creation__rural_pove.mechanism: In Uzbekistan, wetlands formed on drainage channels revived fish, muskrat and reed production, which a project report credits with a substantial income rise for residents [ev_household_income_uzicr_1]. In Australia, cane farmers who built subsidised lagoons were modelled to earn back 0.8 to 1.5 times their costs, and 1.3 to 2.0 times when the raised land could grow cane [ev_wet_eff_cann22_3].
wetland_management__creation__rural_pove.conditionality: The size is not stated. The Uzbek claim is a project self-evaluation that did not measure income, and the wetlands were a by-product of drainage [ev_household_income_uzicr_1]. The Australian figures are a model for a typical farm with the farmer paying only part of construction, and the lower ratio means some farmers would not break even [ev_wet_eff_cann22_3].

wetland_management__creation__soil_erosi.mechanism: A created wetland traps sediment by slowing the water crossing it, and that capacity is finite: as the basin fills, sediment-bound material begins to pass through or discharge again. In the created riverine basins there were signs that sediment and total-phosphorus retention were diminishing after a decade of continuous river flow, while nitrate and soluble-reactive-phosphorus retention persisted (ev_sediment_retention_mits05_5) - the sediment function ages out faster than the nitrogen function.

The row rests on a single narrative statement from a single pair of created basins, and what was observed is a declining sediment-RETENTION service, not measured erosion of land; the authors themselves put it as 'some signs'. It does not say that creating a wetland causes soil loss, only that the trapping benefit should not be assumed to persist without sediment management or maintenance, which belongs in the cost and operations case rather than in the opportunity surface. The setting is a temperate rainfed cropping catchment in a high-income country, pumped continuously from a river, so neither the sediment load nor the maintenance regime transfers to a low- or lower-middle-income landscape without local evidence.

wetland_management__creation__water_qual.mechanism: A created wetland works as a reactor placed in the flow path: residence time rises, nitrogen is removed by plant uptake and denitrification and phosphorus settles with sediment, so a share of the incoming load leaves the water. Where new wetlands are put matters more than how many: modelled placement in the highest nitrogen-surplus areas removes far more nitrogen than placement on non-agricultural land, at a higher cost because it takes cropland out of production (ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_4, ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_2, ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_3), and the gain flattens as restoration spreads beyond the hotspots (ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_5). At site level a created basin exported total phosphorus in its tenth year while its twin barely retained any, after years of consistent retention (ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_4, ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_3), and sediment and total-phosphorus retention were diminishing after a decade of river flow (ev_sediment_retention_mits05_5) - the sediment and phosphorus services age out while the nitrogen service holds. The quantified ceiling claims are modelled, not measured, and every unit is high-income temperate - inflows in the review included treated wastewater and urban runoff as well as agricultural runoff, so the pooled efficiency is not a farmland-only number.

After drains were blocked on an upland bog in Wales, stream flows were higher during dry spells and fell away more slowly than before [ev_water_yield_wils11db_2]. In a computer model of a Canadian river basin, adding wetland area gradually made up for the fall in summer low flows expected under climate change [ev_wet_eff_goy22_2].
wetland_management__drought__all.conditionality: The class is low and no study puts a size on the drought relief. The same Canadian model also found the opposite in places: a restoration scenario made summer low flows worse in some sub-catchments [ev_wet_eff_goy22_3]. Another global analysis gives median project costs of US$1229 for peatlands up to US$89 660 for saltmarsh [ev_project_cost_tail20w1_8, ev_project_cost_tail20w1_6]. wetland_management__fire__all.mechanism: Rewetting moderately reduces fire. Raising the water table in drained peat, mainly by blocking canals, keeps the peat wet so it is harder to ignite. A modelled fire-hazard index in Riau showed continuous extreme hazard 40% less often after rewetting [ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_1], and a planning model put the fall in fire risk at 6%–37% [ev_fire_hazard_tan22_1]. In Malaysia, community patrols together with drain blocking helped cut the extent of forest fires by 98% [ev_fire_hazard_unepgpa22_3]. IPCC, UN and Ramsar guidance and several reviews agree that drained peat is fire-prone and rewetting lowers the risk [ev_fire_hazard_ipcc13wl_2, ev_fire_hazard_unepgpa22_1, ev_wgy_ram_14, ev_fire_hazard_page09_3, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_1]. wetland_management__fire__all.conditionality: The benefit is moderate and fades in the worst years. In the later El Nino of 2023, restored and unrestored peat showed no significant difference [ev_wet_eff_salm26_3]. In the Riau study the area under extreme hazard fell by only 5%, extreme events lasted longer, and the authors say duration was set by the weather, not by rewetting [ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_2, ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_3, ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_4]. At a Central Kalimantan village restoration was largely ineffective, because rewetting was not achieved [ev_wet_eff_mend24_1]. A Sumatran project burned on almost 50% of its area in 2019, which its authors tie to dryland farming on the peat [ev_wet_fire_budi20_2]. Much of the support is guidance or reasoned statements; the Malaysian figure is a single site with patrols in the same package, and the planning model assumes immediate restoration. Most evidence is from Indonesia and Malaysia, and the benefit falls on the landscape, not on a farmer's plot.

A planning model for Indonesian peatlands put the fall in fire risk at 6%–37% [ev_fire_hazard_tan22_1], and a review of Southeast Asian peatlands concludes that raising the water level reduces the risk of fire [ev_fire_hazard_page09_3].
wetland_management__fire__all__aez-humid.conditionality: The class is low. In the Riau study the area under extreme hazard was only 5% lower, extreme events lasted longer in dry El Nino years, and the authors conclude duration was set by the weather, not by rewetting [ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_2, ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_3, ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_4]. IPCC guidance adds that fire is considered unlikely on rewetted organic soils, particularly compared with drained ones [ev_fire_hazard_ipcc13wl_2], and a global review of natural climate solutions lists a lower risk of peat fires as a benefit of rewetting [ev_fire_hazard_griscom17_9].

wetland_management__fire__all__income_gr.mechanism: Rewetting raises the water table and with it the moisture of the fuel: restoring closed-canopy forest vegetation on degraded peatland raises moisture levels in surface and below-ground fire fuels (ev_fire_hazard_mish21_3), and improved hydrology after canal blocking is the stated route to reduced fire hazard (ev_fire_hazard_ritz13_4). wetland_management__flood__all.mechanism: Wetland management moderately reduces flood impacts close to the works. Rewetting and re-roughening land slows storm water, so flood peaks just below the works are lower. On UK peat, peak flows fell 27% where bare peat was re-vegetated, 51% where gullies were also blocked, and 49% at a rewetted gully [ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_O, ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_N, ev_wetflA_gatis_peakflow]. Ditch and drain blocking on Irish and Welsh bogs made stream flow less flashy [ev_flood_hazard_hold04_2, ev_flood_hazard_wils11db_4]. Reconnecting floodplains cut modelled peaks by about 8% to 12% in a base case, and a review puts the average flood-peak cut from river and floodplain measures at 30% [ev_flood_hazard_feder22_2, ev_flood_hazard_bagh25w1_1]. Setting levees back lowered flood levels on large rivers [ev_flood_hazard_knox22_1, ev_flood_hazard_serra22_1]. A Canadian basin model found restored wetland eased the rise in spring flood peaks expected with climate change [ev_wet_eff_goy22_1].

No effect was found across a whole 260 km2 UK catchment, drain blocking is notoriously hard to detect at basin scale, and in major floods the whole basin is saturated so wetlands make no difference [ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_catchment_null, ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_basin_null, ev_wetflA_acre_catastrophic_null]. Placement can reverse the effect: a moorland scheme raised downstream risk, restoring the wrong reach raised flooding upstream, and moving a project downstream turned a 14% peak cut into about a 1% increase [ev_wetflA_shut_synchrony_reversal, ev_flood_hazard_gour20_4, ev_flood_hazard_feder22_4].
