The US figure is a storage calculation, not a flood model or a measured result [ev_flood_hazard_hey95_1]. Both are from high-income countries.
wetland_management__flood_hazard__farmin.agreement_note: Both sources point to less flooding.

wetland_management__flood_hazard__income.mechanism: Studies disagree on whether wetland management lowers or raises flood hazard. On the side of a reduction, wooded wetlands in particular increase flood storage, reduce flood peaks and increase peak travel time [ev_wetflA_acre_wooded_wetland], and a Ramsar briefing note states that wetland protection and restoration buffer communities by reducing wave damage and floods [ev_wet_flood_hazard_ramsar18_2]. On the side of an increase, the same review reports that even where the dominant result is to increase water storage within the wetland, the overall result may still be an increase in flood peaks at the catchment scale [ev_wetflA_acre_synchrony_catchment], and that a change of vegetation from wet meadows to shrubs and trees can double the size and depth of the inundated area for the same size of flood [ev_wetflA_acre_inundation_stage_up].
wetland_management__flood_hazard__income.conditionality: What separates the two sides is scale and position: the reductions are storage and roughness effects on the flood peak passing through or below the wetland [ev_wetflA_acre_wooded_wetland, ev_wet_flood_hazard_ramsar18_2], while the increases arise at catchment scale, where an on-site storage gain need not add up to a downstream benefit [ev_wetflA_acre_synchrony_catchment], and locally, where the roughness that slows the flood raises water level and flooded area on the re-vegetated floodplain itself [ev_wetflA_acre_inundation_stage_up]. The influence of drain blocking on flood flows has been notoriously difficult to detect at the basin scale [ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_basin_null]; and during major catastrophic floods the whole basin may be saturated, so the presence or absence of wetlands, or their management, has no effect [ev_wetflA_acre_catastrophic_null]. None of the units is a measurement of a flood outcome in this scope: they are a single review pooling UK, US, Canadian, Irish and Zimbabwean settings and a global policy brief. Siting matters as much as the practice: whether a wetland intervention lowers flood hazard depends on where it sits in the catchment and how large the flood is.

wetland_management__food_insecurity.mechanism: Restoring seasonal floods brings back fish that households eat and sell. After pilot flood releases on the Waza Logone floodplain in Cameroon, fishing households rose from just over 7,000 to 10,400 and each caught on average 29 sacks of wet fish a year instead of 15 [ev_fish_catch_loth04_2].
wetland_management__food_insecurity.conditionality: The class rests on this single before-and-after account from an IUCN project book, written by project staff (grey literature, no comparison area) [ev_fish_catch_loth04_2]. The only matched evaluation, a wetland restoration project in Uganda, found no significant difference in diet diversity or food insecurity between project and comparison households; that project also restricted access to the wetland [ev_food_security_fp034e_4].
wetland_management__food_insecurity.agreement_note: Sides differ: a large fish-catch gain in Cameroon [ev_fish_catch_loth04_2] against no measurable food-security change in Uganda [ev_food_security_fp034e_4].

wetland_management__heat_stress_hazard.mechanism: Restored wetlands both cool and warm their surroundings, depending on the hour and the season, and both effects are measured. By day they cool by turning incoming energy into evaporation rather than sensible heat: on drained, subsided agricultural peat islands of the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta, three wetlands constructed with managed water tables were significantly cooler by day than a drained alfalfa field on the same peat, by up to 3.4 °C at the young wetland, 5.1 °C at the intermediate one and 2.1 °C at the oldest [ev_microclimate_buffering_hemes18_1]. The energy-balance contrast behind this is illustrated from Trebon, Czech Republic: up to 60% to 70% of solar energy is transformed into sensible heat over a drained crop field against only 5% to 10% over an intact wetland, where 70% to 80% of heat is dissipated via evapotranspiration [ev_wet_microclimate_buffering_ramsar18_1]. By night the same wetlands were warmer than the alfalfa field, by up to 1.9 °C, 3.6 °C and 0.7 °C at the young, intermediate and old sites [ev_microclimate_buffering_hemes18_2], and at the seasonal scale a wetland was up to 2.3 °C warmer than alfalfa, mostly in spring and autumn [ev_microclimate_buffering_hemes18_3].
wetland_management__heat_stress_hazard.conditionality: What separates the two directions is time, not site or method: the warming and the cooling come from the same Delta wetlands measured against the same drained alfalfa field, which is the right baseline for a decision to rewet farmland [ev_microclimate_buffering_hemes18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_hemes18_2]. The cooling is a daytime effect and the warming is a night-time and spring-and-autumn effect [ev_microclimate_buffering_hemes18_3]. Which one matters depends on the heat stress a project targets: daytime heat peaks in the growing season point to the cooling, while night heat or shoulder-season warmth points to the reversal. The paper tests the daytime difference for significance but not the night-time one. All three Delta results are aerodynamic surface temperature, not air temperature, at one temperate delta, and none measures heat stress on people, crops or livestock nearby; the Trebon figures compare an intact wetland with a drained field, not a restored site [ev_wet_microclimate_buffering_ramsar18_1]. Provenance: both sources are high-income temperate settings, the United States and the Czech Republic; no tropical, arid, low-income or lower-middle-income setting is represented, so neither the cooling nor the warming can be assumed to carry over to the target contexts.

wetland_management__peatland__asset_thre.mechanism: Drought damages restored peat by dropping its water table. In a rewetted Indonesian peat restoration area, peat-surface subsidence accelerated sharply during and shortly after the 2019 El Niño drought when groundwater depths were very low, running 2.5 to 4 times the rate of the preceding 3.5 years and more than double the 7.5-year mean (ev_climate_shock_hooi24_5). The authors read their long record as showing that a severe drought could still cause major water-table drops to near 1 m below the peat surface, with carbon-emission spikes, even in otherwise rewetted conditions, in restoration areas and remaining peat-swamp forest alike (ev_climate_shock_hooi24_6). The Ramsar technical guidance records, from its authors' knowledge, that a large number of planted areas in degraded tropical peat-swamp forest have been lost to drought, as well as to fire, flooding and out-competition by ferns and sedges (ev_wgy_ram_22).
wetland_management__peatland__asset_thre.conditionality: Only one unit is a measurement, from one Indonesian site; the second Hooijer unit is the authors' reading of their own record, and the Ramsar statement is expert knowledge with no frequency, site or measurement, made where the guidance itself notes there is very little literature on what happens after planting. The cell is humid-tropical peat in an upper-middle-income setting; no temperate peat and no low-income or lower-middle-income site is represented. Design implication: a rewetting investment in drought-prone tropical peat should expect the asset to lose surface elevation and carbon, and plantings to fail, in El Niño years however well the water management performs, and should budget and monitor for that rather than treat it as a failure of the works.

wetland_management__peatland__biodiversi.mechanism: Raising the water table on drained peat lets peatland plants and animals come back, and actively spreading moss or plants speeds this up. Active restoration with moss transfer brought peat moss and specialist plants close to intact levels within years, while simple rewetting gave slower recovery [ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_7, ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_4]. A review of German fens concludes that rewetting drained fens will increase fen plants and animals, with dry-land species giving way to wetland ones [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tann22_2]. Rewetting a cut-over peatland in Belarus brought reed and sedge back over a large area [ev_wgy_blr_7]. On tropical peat, native swamp trees regrew on their own in the wettest areas [ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3], and an Indonesian model found that restoring lost swamp forest could remove the extinction risk for its forest birds [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tan22_3].
wetland_management__peatland__biodiversi.conditionality: The class is moderate because few results give a size. Restored peat usually stays below intact peat in moss and specialist cover [ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_1]. Leaving peat to recover on its own is projected to take centuries and can stagnate or get worse [ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_5, ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_6]. Rewetting can harm rare dry habitats that have developed on drained peat, a conflict between climate and nature goals [ev_biodiversity_outcome_tann22_3]. The Belarus project missed its own target [ev_wgy_blr_7]. Most evidence is temperate, boreal and high-income; the tropical evidence is thin, partly an expected benefit and partly modelled.
wetland_management__peatland__biodiversi.agreement_note: Most sources report gains; two report harm, from passive restoration and from rewetting rare dry habitats [ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_6, ev_biodiversity_outcome_tann22_3].

wetland_management__peatland__carbon_seq.mechanism: Rewetting peat moderately increases carbon storage. Raising the water table on drained peat stops the stored carbon from rotting away. Over a hundred-year view, rewetting gives net carbon dioxide removal in most peat soils, raises methane, and cuts nitrous oxide and waterborne carbon losses [ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_1]; IPCC guidance puts the median cut in waterborne carbon at 36% and says nitrous oxide falls practically to zero once the water table is within 20 cm of the surface [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc13wl_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc13wl_3]. Each 10 cm the water table is raised cuts net warming by at least 3 tonnes per hectare a year [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_1]. A German scenario of wet farming on fen peat cut emissions in a single state from 5.5 to 1.2 to 3.1 million tonnes a year [ev_carbon_sequestration_tann22_1], and Ramsar guidance holds that, after an early methane peak, rewetting is far better for the climate than staying drained [ev_wgy_ram_1, ev_wgy_ram_3]. Ditch blocking on UK bogs and canal blocking in Kalimantan raised the water table [ev_water_table_depth_hold04_1, ev_water_table_depth_page09_1]. On burned peat in South Sumatra, planted native trees took up 11.3 tonnes of CO2 per hectare a year (Shorea balangeran) and 12.4 tonnes (Dyera polyphylla) in their wood [ev_wet_carbon_budi20_1, ev_wet_carbon_budi20_2]. Reviews of Indonesian peat projects report canal blocks raising the water table: by about 60 cm in the dry season 100 m from a block in Riau, by 70 cm within 170 m of a block at Sungai Tohor, and by a metre over 2420 ha where communities built 12 blocks [ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_2, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_4, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_3].
wetland_management__peatland__carbon_seq.conditionality: The class is moderate because few results give a size. What the peat was drained for matters: rewetting farmed and tropical peat cools quickly, but on forestry-drained peat methane can cancel all the cooling for decades [ev_wgy_ram_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_5]. Water standing above the surface makes methane warming outweigh the carbon saved [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_4]. Partial rewetting slows but does not stop peat loss [ev_carbon_sequestration_unepgpa22_4]. In a Kalimantan simulation, raising water levels gave only a small, not significant fall in carbon dioxide [ev_carbon_sequestration_page09_2], and revegetation on tropical peat has failed: seedlings did no better beside a dammed canal, and aerial seeding survived at about 2% [ev_establishment_survival_page09_6, ev_establishment_survival_pusp21_4]. Much of the evidence is modelled or guidance, mostly from temperate and high-income peat. The South Sumatra tree figures count carbon in the trees only, not the peat below, and come from a single project; the Indonesian water-table results are cited second-hand in a review [ev_wet_carbon_budi20_1, ev_wet_carbon_budi20_2, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_2].

wetland_management__peatland__catchment_.mechanism: Rewetting drained peat restores the water table near the ditch, since restoration and drainage have effects of similar size in opposite directions [ev_wetflA_bring_conclusion]. After drains were blocked on a Welsh bog, stream flows stayed higher and fell away more slowly during dry spells [ev_water_yield_wils11db_2].
wetland_management__peatland__catchment_.conditionality: The size is not stated. Restoration may not reach all the area affected by drainage, and results depend strongly on local conditions [ev_wetflA_bring_conclusion]. Average flows from the same Welsh site fell after blocking, mainly because less time was spent at peak flow [ev_water_yield_wils11db_3]. The evidence is from high-income temperate and boreal peat, and none measures water reaching farmers downstream.
wetland_management__peatland__catchment_.agreement_note: Most results point to more water in dry periods; the same Welsh site shows lower average flows [ev_water_yield_wils11db_3].

wetland_management__peatland__cost_per_h.mechanism: Blocking canals is low-engineering work spread over large areas, which keeps costs in the low thousands of US dollars per hectare: Indonesia's rewetting programme is estimated at US$2,300/ha [ev_wgy_ram_19], a review of Indonesian studies puts restoration mostly between US$500 and US$2,500 per ha [ev_wet_cost_jali25_1], and modelled and project figures fall between US$1625/ha and US$1866/ha [ev_wet_cost_jali25_2, ev_wet_cost_jali25_3, ev_project_cost_alex26_1]. Replanting burned peat costs around 1100 USD/ha [ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_7].
wetland_management__peatland__cost_per_h.conditionality: All figures are from Indonesia, an upper-middle-income country, so no cost class is given for lower-income settings. Most are second-hand planning estimates or models without a price year [ev_wgy_ram_19, ev_wet_cost_jali25_2]. Replanting does not guarantee success [ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_7]. Read them as a scale, not a budget.

wetland_management__peatland__cost_reduc.mechanism: Farming a rewetted peatland costs more than farming it drained: wet cultivation brings higher risk, high investment costs and the need for specialised harvesting equipment and adapted production [ev_wet_cost_neud26_3]. At the high-input extreme, establishing a Sphagnum production field on former bog grassland, calculated from pilot cost data in 2011 and 2016, cost in the order of a hundred thousand euros per hectare, lower at the later date [ev_wgy_wich_7].
wetland_management__peatland__cost_reduc.conditionality: European evidence only (German pilot plus a scoping review whose economics corpus is mostly European). The Sphagnum figures describe topsoil removal, pumped irrigation and specialised machinery, far beyond simple ditch blocking; low-input rewetting would cost far less, but no source here quantifies it.

wetland_management__peatland__drought__a.mechanism: Blocking the drains on a damaged upland bog in Wales kept stream flows higher during dry spells, and flows fell away more slowly than before blocking [ev_water_yield_wils11db_2].
wetland_management__peatland__drought__a.conditionality: This rests on a single study at a single site, so the size of the benefit is not stated [ev_water_yield_wils11db_2]. The dry spells were short, not a serious drought, and the setting is a temperate, high-income upland. The benefit is in the stream downstream, not on farmland.
wetland_management__peatland__drought__a.agreement_note: A single measured study, so agreement between sources cannot be judged.

wetland_management__peatland__establishm.mechanism: Peat rewetting is the cheap end of wetland establishment. A compiled global database puts peatland restoration at $1,094 per hectare per year [ev_project_cost_rgwo25_3], and another analysis gives a median of US$1229 [ev_project_cost_tail20w1_8]. In Indonesia a canal block costs about 300 US$, whether of compacted peat or local wood and sandbags [ev_project_cost_hooi24_4, ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_6].
wetland_management__peatland__establishm.conditionality: The per-hectare figures are total project costs spread over time; the block cost is per structure, and how many blocks a site needs is not given. The block costs are from Indonesia (upper-middle income), and the database figures do not give countries. None is a low-income cost.

wetland_management__peatland__fire__all.mechanism: Rewetting moderately reduces fire. Raising the water table in drained peat, mainly by blocking canals, keeps the peat wet so it is harder to ignite. In a national comparison in Indonesia during the El Nino of 2019, peat restored with canal dams had fewer fire hotspots than matched unrestored peat (5 against 6 per square kilometre) [ev_wet_eff_salm26_1]. A modelled fire-hazard index in Riau showed continuous extreme hazard 40% less often after rewetting [ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_1], and a planning model put the fall in fire risk at 6%–37% [ev_fire_hazard_tan22_1]. In Malaysia, community patrols together with drain blocking helped cut the extent of forest fires by 98% [ev_fire_hazard_unepgpa22_3]. A review notes that undrained peat swamp forest stays moist and is at very low fire risk, while drained peat next to farmland carries the greatest risk [ev_fire_hazard_jauhiainen16_4]. A global review of natural climate solutions also lists a lower risk of peat fires as a benefit of rewetting, citing earlier work second-hand [ev_fire_hazard_griscom17_9].
wetland_management__peatland__fire__all.conditionality: The benefit is moderate and fades in the worst years. In the El Nino of 2023, restored and unrestored peat showed no significant difference [ev_wet_eff_salm26_3]. In the Riau study the area under extreme hazard fell by only 5%, extreme events lasted longer, and the authors say duration was set by the weather [ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_2, ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_3, ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_4]. At a Central Kalimantan village, restoration was largely ineffective because rewetting was not achieved [ev_wet_eff_mend24_1]. A Sumatran project burned on almost 50% of its area in 2019, which its authors tie to dryland farming on the peat [ev_wet_fire_budi20_2]. IPCC guidance warns that fire risk on rewetted soils may still be real [ev_fire_hazard_ipcc13wl_2]. The forest-versus-drained comparison describes existing peat, not restored peat, and the Malaysian figure is a single site with patrols in the same package. Most evidence is from Indonesia and Malaysia, and the benefit falls on the landscape, not on a farmer's plot.

wetland_management__peatland__flood__all.mechanism: Re-vegetating bare peat and blocking drains and gullies slows storm water. Peak flow fell 27% where bare peat was re-vegetated, 51% where gullies were also blocked, and 49% at a rewetted gully [ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_O, ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_N, ev_wetflA_gatis_peakflow]. Ditch blocking on an Irish bog gave flow close to that of undamaged bog, and drain blocking on a Welsh bog made stream flow significantly less flashy [ev_flood_hazard_hold04_2, ev_flood_hazard_wils11db_4]. Loss of vegetation and drainage go with higher, faster flood peaks [ev_wetflA_dads_degradation_loss, ev_wetflA_acre_barepeat_loss].
wetland_management__peatland__flood__all.conditionality: The class is moderate because only a few results give a size, and the benefit is shown at small scale. No effect was found across a whole 260 km2 catchment, and modelled land changes cut an extreme peak by a median of only 2% [ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_catchment_null, ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_model_2pct]. In the Welsh study the fall in stream peak flow was not significant [ev_flood_hazard_wils11db_4]. Bogs that are wet most of the year rarely hold back flow, and a moorland scheme raised downstream risk by lining up flood peaks [ev_wetflA_acre_saturated_bog_reversal, ev_wetflA_shut_synchrony_reversal]. At the rewetted gully the peak fell but water arrived faster [ev_wetflA_gatis_lag_reversal]. Almost all evidence is UK blanket bog, temperate and high-income, and the benefit arrives downstream.
wetland_management__peatland__flood__all.agreement_note: Most site results show lower or slower peaks; several sources find no effect at larger scale, and three report flooding made worse in some settings [ev_wetflA_acre_saturated_bog_reversal, ev_wetflA_shut_synchrony_reversal, ev_wetflA_gatis_lag_reversal].

wetland_management__peatland__production.mechanism: Rewetting peat ends drainage-based cropping: crops such as potatoes and carrots become unsuitable, drained and wet uses cannot share a peatland, and wet-farming crops are mostly not food [ev_wgy_qa_6, ev_wgy_ram_17, ev_wet_cropyield_temm26_5]. Rewetting arable fen in England caused a large loss of arable food production, partly offset by grazing [ev_agricultural_production_value_rgwo25_2]. Keeping tropical peat drained also loses production in the long run, as the land subsides and drainage fails [ev_agricultural_production_value_hooi12_3, ev_agricultural_production_value_ritz13_9].
wetland_management__peatland__production.conditionality: The size is not stated. In Finland the national effect was judged minor, with local problems [ev_wgy_qa_5]. Most Sumatran smallholders with a canal block noticed no impact on yields [ev_crop_yield_ward20_1]. Most of the loss evidence is European expert statements. The likely pattern is a production cost now, with larger losses possibly avoided later on deep, sinking tropical peat.
wetland_management__peatland__production.agreement_note: Most sources point to lost crop production now; Sumatran farmers mostly noticed no change [ev_crop_yield_ward20_1].

wetland_management__peatland__recurrent_.mechanism: A global meta-analysis of wetland restoration costs gives peatland restoration a median total project cost of US$1229 per hectare per year of the restoration event, in 2010 US$, the lowest of the wetland types it compares [ev_project_cost_tail20w1_8].
wetland_management__peatland__recurrent_.conditionality: Those Taillardat medians are not running costs: they are total project costs spread over the duration of the restoration event, with one-off events counted as a single year, so they belong with establishment cost and must not be read as a yearly maintenance bill. They are 2010 US dollar medians over actual and planned projects. The peatland median comes from a small set of projects whose countries the text does not state. No recurrent peatland cost - dam maintenance, water-level management, forgone farm income - is measured in this row.

wetland_management__peatland__rural_pove.mechanism: On rewetted peat, income holds up or rises where a product sells or a payment is made. High-value products such as thatching reed and peat moss for growers can pay [ev_wet_econret_neud26_2, ev_wgy_wich_6], German fen wet pastures with hardy breeds were profitable in all scenarios [ev_economic_return_tann22_4], and in Viet Nam alternative fire-free livelihoods doubled annual incomes [ev_wet_hhinc_terz22_1]. Converting German arable land to grassland and rewetting it raised gross margin by 5% on average [ev_wet_hhinc_meye26_2]. In South Sumatra, a cited study found native peat-swamp trees (Shorea balangeran and Dyera polyphylla) worth more than the current practice of burning to plant sonor rice [ev_wet_econret_budi20_2].
wetland_management__peatland__rural_pove.conditionality: The gain is slight and losses are common. Wet farming is generally not profitable on biomass sales alone [ev_wet_econret_neud26_1]; German farms rewetting grassland lost 35% of gross margin on average [ev_wet_hhinc_meye26_1]; Southeast Asian oil palm communities face lower returns [ev_household_income_mish21_5]; and an Indonesian review says existing livelihoods will no longer be feasible on rewetted peat [ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_5]. Wicken Fen's benefit-cost ratio of 4.4 against 1.3 for farming counts public benefits, not household income [ev_economic_return_rgwo25_1]. The gains are mostly modelled or self-reported, and the German profits include payments [ev_economic_return_tann22_4]. The key question for a project is whether a product or a payment can replace lost farm income. The South Sumatra comparison is second-hand and gives no figure [ev_wet_econret_budi20_2].

wetland_management__peatland__soil_erosi.mechanism: Re-vegetating bare blanket peat, alone or together with gully blocking by stone and timber dams, is the peatland practice behind this row. On the only quantity measured here - the share of storm rainfall leaving as storm discharge - restoration changed nothing at either restored site relative to the bare, unrestored control (ev_wetflA_shut_runoffcoef_null).
wetland_management__peatland__soil_erosi.conditionality: The no-relationship class rests on that null alone, and it is about water volume, not soil. The unit behind this row is a runoff-coefficient null (ev_wetflA_shut_runoffcoef_null), and the paper's own conclusion is that restoration altered the timing and peak of storm delivery while leaving the volume of runoff produced unchanged. It is therefore evidence that re-vegetation and gully blocking did not reduce how much water ran off, and it should not be read as evidence that they fail to reduce erosion - no sediment or soil-loss measurement is present in this pool, which is why the cell states no relationship rather than a reduction, and the row stands as an evidence gap. The observation comes from an upland English blanket-peat site in a high-income temperate setting, with no tropical peat and no farmland, so this row marks an evidence gap rather than a finding of no effect.

wetland_management__peatland__water_qual.mechanism: Rewetting a cut-over peat site - raising the water table, filling or blocking ditches, mulching and transferring a moss layer - stabilises the water table and keeps the exposed peat saturated, so less nutrient and carbon load is flushed from the surface. Against the realistic do-nothing counterfactual of an abandoned extraction site, the loads leaving restored sites were lower (ev_nutrient_removal_rasa23_5). The Ramsar technical report, citing the literature, generalises this: disturbed peatlands release substantial quantities of humic acids, nitrogen, sulphur, heavy metals and suspended solids, whereas drain-blocking generally leads to a substantial reduction in their outflow (ev_wgy_ram_6, ev_wgy_ram_7).
wetland_management__peatland__water_qual.conditionality: The gain is measured against the degraded starting point, and against that baseline restored extraction sites leak less (ev_nutrient_removal_rasa23_5). Measured against their intact natural counterparts the same restored sites leaked more nutrients and carbon, associated with greater water-table variation (ev_nutrient_removal_rasa23_4); that is incomplete recovery towards an intact peatland, not harm, and the two comparisons must not be netted. The real reversals are in the Ramsar report's cited synthesis. In some cases restoration causes a temporarily increased flush of nutrients into downstream water courses, though the release decreases in the longer term (ev_wgy_ram_8); and on nutrient-rich, formerly fertilised agricultural fens, rewetting may even increase the nutrient problem by mobilising hitherto bound phosphorus and nitrogen, internal eutrophication (ev_wgy_ram_9). Agricultural peat is exactly the land a rural scan would target, so a downstream nutrient pulse in the early years, and a sustained phosphorus problem on fertilised fens, should be planned for rather than assumed away. The measured case in this pool found no significant water-quality improvement and no significant reduction in aqueous carbon losses after rewetting an eroding upland blanket peat, with dissolved organic carbon rising non-significantly afterwards (ev_wetflA_gatis_waterquality_null); the quantity measured there is dissolved organic carbon routed to the nearest water-quality outcome, not nutrients, and water colour did change. Everything here is boreal or temperate peat in high-income countries or unspecified settings; nothing covers tropical peat or a farmed low- or lower-middle-income catchment, and the Ramsar statements give direction without magnitude or site.

wetland_management__peatland__water_stre.mechanism: On peat, rewetting puts the water table back towards where the drain took it from. On an eroding English upland peatland, peat barriers built across gullies raised mean water tables significantly at every distance class, in the peat pans from 0.003 m below ground level to 0.064 m above it and in the vegetated haggs from 0.188 to 0.175 m below ground within 0.5 m of the pan edge [ev_wetflA_gatis_watertable]. On cutaway peat, the water-table level was successfully recovered by active restoration through ditch blocking and dam construction [ev_water_regulation_rasa23_6]. In tropical peat the same holds behind canal dams, reported in a review of Indonesian restoration techniques (Dohong et al.): the water table within the dammed sites in the SSI canal, Sebangau National Park, remained above the threshold level of 40 cm below the peat surface during the dry year 2006, while the unblocked control canal fell significantly below it (Panda et al. 2012) [ev_water_regulation_doh18_1], and the water table within the Kalampangan canals increased up to 151 cm following dam installation (Limin et al. 2007) [ev_water_regulation_doh18_2]. A basin-scale model of rewetting drained peat in the Neman basin (Stachowicz et al.) puts the extra water retained at 69 to 344 m3·ha−1, or 23.6–118 M m3 across the basin [ev_water_regulation_sta22_1].
wetland_management__peatland__water_stre.conditionality: The meta-analytic near-ditch groundwater result now sits in the peatland catchment water yield row. The English rise is in the mean rather than the typical state: median water-table conditions remained similar at all distances after restoration, so the significant mean rise is driven by the wet tail [ev_wetflA_gatis_watertable]. Water-table fluctuation and the moisture dynamics of the peat layer were found difficult to maintain in restored peat-extraction areas, so the level returns but its dynamics do not [ev_water_regulation_rasa23_7]; and many hydrological processes do not fully recover within the first years after restoration, because degradation has already changed peat structure and consolidation, so early results are not the steady state and the monitoring windows behind most restoration claims are shorter than the recovery time [ev_wetflA_acre_recovery_timescale]. The Indonesian results are cited second-hand from single canal systems, a before-after rise and a dammed-against-unblocked comparison through a dry year [ev_water_regulation_doh18_1, ev_water_regulation_doh18_2]. The Neman model is a scenario estimate, and its basin total corresponds to 0.14–0.7% of the total annual Neman River discharge into the Baltic Sea - water held in the peat, not delivered to users [ev_water_regulation_sta22_1]. Apart from the Indonesian canal cases the units are temperate or boreal, from the UK, Ireland, Canada, Fennoscandia and northern Europe; none is from a low- or lower-middle-income setting, and none measures water available to a farming system or water stress experienced by farmers.

wetland_management__production_gap.mechanism: Wetland management has been found both to cut and to raise farm production. Where floods return to grazing land, livestock gain: after pilot flood releases in Cameroon the breeding rate of cows rose from 16% to 50% [ev_livestock_productivity_loth04_1], and reopening a creek in Ghana enhanced cattle farming [ev_livestock_productivity_ghppar_2]. Where farmed land is rewetted, crop output falls: rewetted peat becomes unsuitable for crops such as potatoes and carrots [ev_wgy_qa_6, ev_wgy_ram_17]; wet-farming crops are mostly not food [ev_wet_cropyield_temm26_5]; and rewetting arable fen in England caused a large loss of arable food production, partly offset by more grazing [ev_agricultural_production_value_rgwo25_2]. Near Poyang Lake, tenant farmers' crops are damaged by protected birds with no compensation [ev_wgy_poy_2].
wetland_management__production_gap.conditionality: What separates the sides is what the land was used for. Losses come where cropland on drained peat or lakebed is rewetted; gains come where seasonal floods return to grazing land [ev_agricultural_production_value_rgwo25_2, ev_livestock_productivity_loth04_1]. The loss can be local rather than national: Finland expects only a minor national effect [ev_wgy_qa_5]. Several measured studies found no change: a matched Uganda evaluation found no significant yield change, and most Sumatran smallholders with a canal block noticed no impact, though about 10% reported lower yields [ev_crop_yield_fp034e_5, ev_crop_yield_ward20_1]. Much of the loss side is European expert statement; the Cameroon gain is a project's own grey-literature account with no comparison area.
wetland_management__production_gap.agreement_note: Gains: livestock in Cameroon and Ghana [ev_livestock_productivity_loth04_1, ev_livestock_productivity_ghppar_2]. Losses: crops on rewetted peat and near protected wetlands [ev_agricultural_production_value_rgwo25_2, ev_wgy_qa_6, ev_wgy_poy_2]. No change: Uganda and Sumatra [ev_crop_yield_fp034e_5, ev_crop_yield_ward20_1].

wetland_management__production_gap__inco.mechanism: Rewetting farmed peat replaces food crops with mostly non-food wet crops, which can mean a local loss of food production [ev_wet_cropyield_temm26_5]. Rewetting arable fen at Wicken Fen in England caused a large loss of arable food production, partly offset by more livestock grazing [ev_agricultural_production_value_rgwo25_2].
wetland_management__production_gap__inco.conditionality: The size is not stated. In Finland the national effect was judged minor, with problems concentrated in peat-rich districts [ev_wgy_qa_5]. The sources are reviews and a grey-literature restatement of a valuation, not measured farm outcomes. The loss falls on the farms whose land is rewetted.
wetland_management__production_gap__inco.agreement_note: All three sources point to lost production.

wetland_management__production_gap__inco.mechanism: Returning floods to grazing land improves pasture. After pilot flood releases on the Waza Logone floodplain in Cameroon, the breeding rate of cows rose from 16% to 50%, and of small ruminants from 32% to 50% [ev_livestock_productivity_loth04_1]. In Ghana, clearing a creek to reconnect a lagoon was said to enhance cattle farming along it [ev_livestock_productivity_ghppar_2].
wetland_management__production_gap__inco.conditionality: The Cameroon figures come from repeated surveys with no comparison area in a project book written by project staff, and the authors say only that the rise coincided with the releases [ev_livestock_productivity_loth04_1]. The Ghana claim is from evaluation interviews [ev_livestock_productivity_ghppar_2]. The only matched study, in Uganda, found no significant change in crop yield [ev_crop_yield_fp034e_5]. Gains appear where floods return to grazing land, not on crops.
wetland_management__production_gap__inco.agreement_note: Livestock gains in Cameroon and Ghana; no significant crop change in Uganda [ev_crop_yield_fp034e_5].

wetland_management__production_gap__inco.mechanism: Near the protected Poyang Lake wetland in China, crops of farmers who rent land are damaged by migratory birds and other wild animals, and these tenants get no compensation [ev_wgy_poy_2]. In Sumatra, among smallholders who already had a canal block to rewet their peat, 9.7% reported lower crop yields and 12.9% found it harder to reach their farms [ev_crop_yield_ward20_1].
wetland_management__production_gap__inco.conditionality: The size is not stated and the evidence is weak. Most Sumatran smallholders with a canal block (61.3%) noticed no impact at all, and the answers are self-reported [ev_crop_yield_ward20_1]. The Poyang finding is from a household survey that does not separate restoration from wildlife protection [ev_wgy_poy_2]. Paying compensation to the people who actually farm the land would address the Poyang problem.
wetland_management__production_gap__inco.agreement_note: Poyang points to lost crops; most Sumatran farmers noticed no change [ev_wgy_poy_2, ev_crop_yield_ward20_1].

wetland_management__recurrent_cost.mechanism: Two kinds of recurring cost sit in this pool. The first is a land payment in a US national model: where wetlands are restored on farmland, land rental costs cover the opportunity cost of land removed from agricultural production, and for cropland they are, in the mean, more than five times greater than those for pastureland, at US$274 ± 156 per hectare [ev_project_cost_cheng20_6]. Design, construction and maintenance enter the same framework as area-dependent costs annualised over a 50-year management horizon at a real discount rate of 4%, with the rental rates taken from state-level agricultural statistics across the 48 contiguous states. The second is upkeep: evidence compiled in the cost-effectiveness review suggests that annual monitoring costs are typically around 20% of the initial restoration investment for floodplain restoration in the USA, and mangrove restoration in the Philippines and Vietnam [ev_project_cost_tail20w1_11].
wetland_management__recurrent_cost.conditionality: This is a modelled national cost framework for constructed nutrient-retention wetlands, and the recurring item prices forgone agriculture on US cropland, a high-income economy; it cannot be read across to a low- or lower-middle-income landscape, where the opportunity cost of farmland is set by quite different land and tenure arrangements. No currency year is stated in the quoted passage. The monitoring share is a cited summary, not a measurement from these projects, and it is expressed relative to the initial investment, so it scales with however large that establishment cost was. The useful point is structural: where wetlands are restored on farmland, the standing cost is the production forgone, not the upkeep of the works. The Taillardat per-hectare-per-year medians formerly pooled here are total project capital annualised over the restoration event and now sit in establishment cost (the cost-routing rule) [ev_project_cost_cheng20_6].

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: Drought can switch off the flood pulse a restored floodplain depends on. On a restored floodplain the hazard works by removing the flood the wetland depends on: in 2020, lack of snow cover and severe drought meant no spring flooding on the Pripyat floodplain, and migrating and nesting birds on the restored floodplain meadows declined strongly (ev_wgy_blr_6).
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: This is one observation in a project terminal evaluation from Belarus, an upper-middle-income temperate setting, and the practice is restoration and maintenance of open floodplain meadows by grazing and mowing, not rewetting of drained land; the indicator is the number of migrating and nesting birds, not a livelihood or a hydrological measure, and the evaluation gives no size for the decline. It also names drought and snowless winters as arriving faster and more severely than the project was designed for. The lesson that transfers is a design one: a floodplain wetland fed by a seasonal flood is exposed whenever drought removes that flood, so its habitat function, and anything that depends on it, should be expected to fail in such years.

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: Restoring water to a degraded wetland strongly increases biodiversity. Reinstating hydrology on a degraded wetland puts back standing water and saturated soil, and the gain is measured against that degraded starting point. How degraded that point is comes from a review of agricultural use of wetlands, restating the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment: natural wetlands reclaimed by drainage and land amelioration have lost much of their original character, leading to reduced biodiversity and reduced performance of functions other than crop productivity (ev_biodiversity_outcome_verh09_5). That unit describes what reclaiming an existing wetland cost, not a restoration result; it enters this family row through the existing-wetland home-family route, as a statement of the degraded starting point rather than a measured restoration outcome. Restoring degraded wetlands enhanced biodiversity overall and the diversity of vertebrates, vascular plants and terrestrial and aquatic invertebrates (ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_3). The mobile parts of the system return soonest: vertebrate assemblages reached reference structural values within a few years (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_6), and riverine and tidal wetlands kept connected by natural flow variation recovered biogeochemical function and biological structure after 20 and 30 years respectively (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_9). Project cases show the same fast early response. After the first test flooding of the restored Belene Island marshes, park reports cited by the World Bank record fish species rising from 2 to 10 within 2 months and ferruginous duck nesting pairs from 5 to 50 (ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_1); a project-supported inventory found flora and fauna beginning to regenerate after the Lapusna wetland in Moldova was restored (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mdicr_2). Reconnecting floodplains by setting levees back works the same way: a critical review of levee alteration (Knox et al.) reports reduced flood stages and improved biodiversity after a setback on the Missouri River in Iowa (Smith et al.) (ev_biodiversity_outcome_knox22_1) and a setback on the Elbe in Germany was followed by newly established floodplain forest and excavated shallow water bodies, with the documented return of many waterfowl and other bird species and a diversity of habitat types (Serra-Llobet et al.) (ev_biodiversity_outcome_serra22_2). On California's unregulated Cosumnes River, partial levee removal and setback reconnected the river to its floodplain, and the renewed flooding diversified flow and geomorphology, promoted riparian vegetation establishment and supported positive responses from native fish and the aquatic ecosystem (ev_biodiversity_outcome_serra22_5). A review of floodplain wetland restoration studies finds the same direction in how projects report themselves: most published studies deemed their restoration activities successful or partially successful, irrespective of the restoration activity performed (ev_biodiversity_outcome_maxw26w1_1). The Lao and Sierra Leone units come from protecting existing wetlands rather than restoring them: in Lao PDR, designating fishery conservation zones was followed by an increase in native fish populations and more fish for local consumption (ev_wgy_lao_3), and at Sierra Leone's Mamunta Mayosso sanctuary positive changes in biodiversity conservation are confirmed after cattle settlements were banned (ev_biodiversity_outcome_wcpsl_1).
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: A restored wetland that falls short of an intact one is a recovery note, not harm, and it is kept apart from the gain above. The slow parts lag: plant assemblages took decades to converge statistically with reference sites and their absolute structural values remained below reference even 100 years after restoration, with biological structure and biogeochemical functioning still lower than reference (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_7, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_1), while inland depressional wetlands fed only by precipitation or groundwater had not recovered to reference conditions decades after restoration (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_8). The global syntheses disagree on whether that shortfall persists, since biodiversity in restored wetlands did not significantly differ from that in natural wetlands (ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_2). Not every group responds: macroinvertebrate diversity showed no significant effect (ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_4), and a cited North American case found that restoring individual wetlands did not bring back the Topeka Shiner, a small fish; the authors argue species moving between wetlands need restoration across many wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_maxw26w1_3]. The project units are weaker than their numbers suggest. The Bulgarian counts are park reports taken within months of the first flooding (ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_bgicr_2), and the Moldovan result is direction only (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mdicr_2). The Missouri entry is a second-hand table row, direction only (ev_biodiversity_outcome_knox22_1). The Elbe and Cosumnes findings are case studies with a before/after framing and no control site, and the Elbe bird counts are project-success evaluations cited without a named underlying study (ev_biodiversity_outcome_serra22_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_serra22_5). On a different reconnected floodplain, on the Bear River, hydraulic modelling found most of the reconnected area would flood only in a 2-year event and so would not provide the frequent, long-duration inundated habitat that native fish need — a design limitation on that one project, not a finding against reconnection generally [ev_biodiversity_outcome_serra22_4]. The floodplain review is a vote count of authors' own declared success against indicators they chose, not a measured effect against a baseline, and its authors warn that unsuccessful outcomes are likely under-reported (ev_biodiversity_outcome_maxw26w1_1); it also relays a before-and-after study in which hydrological restoration of inundation levels failed to restore invertebrate food sources for birds, likely because of vague aims and predictions of what the target species required (ev_biodiversity_outcome_maxw26w1_2). The Sierra Leone claim is an evaluator's assertion about a bundle of grazing by-laws, boundary demarcation and co-management, and it depended on the exit of all Fula settlements and their cattle, a livelihood cost the biodiversity gain does not show (ev_biodiversity_outcome_wcpsl_1). The Lao result rests on project fish-monitoring records inside protected zones (ev_wgy_lao_3). The comparisons against intact reference sites (ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_6, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_7, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_8, ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_9) are held out of the class for that reason: they measure how far recovery has to go, not what restoration adds over the degraded starting point.

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: Rewetting degraded wetlands cuts greenhouse-gas emissions because carbon dioxide uptake more than offsets the methane and nitrous oxide [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_3]; emissions are lowest when the water table sits near the surface [ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_4]. Measurements on restored wetlands on drained Californian peat showed a net greenhouse-gas benefit in some cases [ev_carbon_sequestration_hemes18_5]. A global meta-analysis found methane rose by 122.3% after restoration, yet total emissions were no higher than in disturbed wetlands [ev_carbon_sequestration_xu25_3]. Restored forested wetlands on former US farmland were modelled to store 15.8 to 92.4 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per hectare every five years [ev_carbon_sequestration_jenk10_1].
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: The size is not stated and methane is the trade-off. Restored freshwater marshes gain soil carbon at the cost of significant methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_hemes18_4], and restored wetlands can warm the climate for their first years to decades, with the switch to net cooling estimated at 57 to 299 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_4]. Converting a natural riverside wetland to pasture lowered its warming effect in a meta-analysis, a reminder that keeping land wet has a methane cost [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan20_3]. Most evidence is from the United States and other high-income settings, and the benefit goes to the climate, not to the farmer.
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.agreement_note: Most sources show net gains; two show warming over some period [ev_carbon_sequestration_tail20w1_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_tan20_3].

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: Ditch blocking raised groundwater by 22 cm near the work across boreal and temperate wetlands [ev_wetflA_bring_gw_rise]. In a Canadian basin model, adding wetland area gradually offset the fall in summer low flows expected under climate change [ev_wet_eff_goy22_2]. A global review finds some floodplain wetlands recharge groundwater when flooded [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_bull03_10].
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: The size is not stated and the evidence pulls both ways. The groundwater rise is local and effects beyond the wetland could not be judged [ev_wetflA_bring_gw_decay, ev_wetflA_bring_outside_inconclusive]. The global review of existing wetlands finds that most studies show wetlands increase evaporation and reduce annual and dry-season river flow, and about as many recharge groundwater less than surrounding land as more [ev_water_yield_bull03_5, ev_water_yield_bull03_8, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_bull03_11]. In the Canadian model, a restoration scenario made low flows worse in some sub-catchments [ev_wet_eff_goy22_3]. Much of this is about existing wetlands, not restored ones, mostly in high-income settings.
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.agreement_note: Restoration-site results point to more water; the global review of existing wetlands and part of the Canadian model point to less river flow [ev_water_yield_bull03_5, ev_water_yield_bull03_8, ev_wet_eff_goy22_3].

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: Reconnecting floodplains costs what the water-control works and planting cost: US$1,903/ha for controlled flooding of Danube marshes in Bulgaria [ev_project_cost_bgieg_1], $3200 ha-1 for wetland planting in Vermont [ev_project_cost_gour20_5], and about $680 to $900/ha to restore forested wetland on US farmland [ev_project_cost_jenk10_3].
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: All figures are high-income with no price year. The US figures leave out land [ev_project_cost_gour20_5, ev_project_cost_jenk10_3]. No local cost evidence for low-income settings.

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: Wetlands hold water through the wet season and release it slowly, which can keep a river flowing, or grass growing, after the rain stops. In a model of a river basin in northeast China, wetlands beside rivers eased drought and helped keep low flows going during the severe drought of 2011 [ev_drought_hazard_wu23_2, ev_drought_hazard_wu23_6]. A review of African wetlands says they are essential dry-season grazing for wild and domestic animals, helping herds through severe dry seasons and droughts [ev_drought_hazard_fyn15_1]. An IUCN project report on the Waza Logone floodplain in Cameroon says the presence of floods helps reduce the impacts and severity of drought [ev_drought_hazard_loth04_7]. In a Canadian basin model, adding wetland area gradually made up for climate-driven falls in summer low flows [ev_wet_eff_goy22_2].
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: The class is low and no source gives a size. The models also show harm: isolated wetlands in the Chinese basin could deepen the drought shortfall [ev_drought_hazard_wu23_3], and a Canadian restoration scenario made summer low flows worse in some sub-catchments [ev_wet_eff_goy22_3]. Little of this is about restored wetlands: the Chinese model removes existing wetlands, and the African review and the Cameroon report describe existing floodplains and their natural floods [ev_drought_hazard_wu23_2, ev_drought_hazard_fyn15_1, ev_drought_hazard_loth04_7]. The Cameroon statement is the project's own assessment in grey literature. None of it was measured in the field. The benefit reaches river users downstream, and herders who can move stock onto the wetland, rather than the land where the work is done.
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.agreement_note: Most results point to drought relief; isolated wetlands and a restoration scenario made dry-season flows worse [ev_drought_hazard_wu23_3, ev_wet_eff_goy22_3].

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: Wetlands hold water through the wet season and release it slowly, which keeps grass growing for livestock after the rain stops. A review of African wetlands says they are essential dry-season grazing for wild and domestic animals, helping herds through severe dry seasons and droughts [ev_drought_hazard_fyn15_1]. An IUCN project report on the Waza Logone floodplain in Cameroon says the presence of floods helps reduce the impacts and severity of drought [ev_drought_hazard_loth04_7]. Basin models in China and Canada add that wetlands can help keep rivers flowing in dry periods [ev_drought_hazard_wu23_6, ev_wet_eff_goy22_2].
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: The class is low and no source gives a size. The models also show harm: isolated wetlands in the Chinese basin could deepen the drought shortfall [ev_drought_hazard_wu23_3], and a Canadian restoration scenario made summer low flows worse in some sub-catchments [ev_wet_eff_goy22_3]. The evidence is mostly about existing wetlands and natural floods, not restored ones; the Cameroon statement is the project's own grey-literature assessment, and nothing was measured in the field [ev_drought_hazard_loth04_7]. For herders, the closest evidence is the African review and the Cameroon floodplain; the river-basin models describe no farming system and are pooled here as the only other drought evidence.
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.agreement_note: Most results point to drought relief; isolated wetlands and a restoration scenario made dry-season flows worse [ev_drought_hazard_wu23_3, ev_wet_eff_goy22_3].

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: Wetlands hold water through the wet season and release it slowly. In a model of a basin in northeast China, wetlands beside rivers eased drought and helped keep low flows going in the severe drought of 2011 [ev_drought_hazard_wu23_2, ev_drought_hazard_wu23_6]. A review of African wetlands says they are essential dry-season grazing that helps herds through droughts [ev_drought_hazard_fyn15_1]. An IUCN project report on the Waza Logone floodplain in Cameroon says the presence of floods helps reduce the impacts and severity of drought [ev_drought_hazard_loth04_7].
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: The size is not stated. In the same Chinese model, isolated wetlands could deepen the drought shortfall [ev_drought_hazard_wu23_3]. The evidence is about existing wetlands and natural floods, not restored ones: the model removes existing wetlands, and the review and Cameroon report describe existing floodplains [ev_drought_hazard_wu23_2, ev_drought_hazard_fyn15_1, ev_drought_hazard_loth04_7]. The Cameroon statement is the project's own assessment in grey literature, and nothing was measured in the field. Benefits reach river users downstream and herders who can move stock onto the wetland.
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.agreement_note: Sources point to drought relief, except isolated wetlands in the Chinese model [ev_drought_hazard_wu23_3].

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: Marsh and floodplain restoration needs more water engineering, such as weirs, and costs more: a compiled global database puts inland marshes and swamps at $24,308 per hectare per year [ev_project_cost_rgwo25_4], and another analysis gives medians of US$71 221 for freshwater marsh and US$20 948 for floodplains [ev_project_cost_tail20w1_9, ev_project_cost_tail20w1_7].
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: These are total project costs spread over time, not running costs. The marsh projects were in high-income countries and the floodplain figure rests on a single project. No low-income cost is available.

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: A groundwater model for Central Kalimantan compares relatively intact peat swamp forest with a drained, burnt block of the former Mega Rice Project. In a dry year, the water table fell below the depth at which surface peat can ignite on 15% of the intact peat, against 85% of the drained block [ev_fire_hazard_page09_4].
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: There is not enough evidence to set a class. This is a single modelled study comparing existing intact peat with drained peat; it does not measure rewetting [ev_fire_hazard_page09_4]. It shows why drained peat burns, not how much restoration reduces fire. A second independent source, or a measured result after rewetting, is needed.

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: Reconnecting and rewetting floodplains gives storm water somewhere to spread outside the channel. Modelled peak flow fell by up to 37% along a reconnected reach [ev_flood_hazard_feder22_1]; hollow wetlands could store 72% of the runoff from a 2-year storm [ev_wetflA_acre_depression_storage]; and embanking a floodplain raised the modelled downstream peak by 57% [ev_wetflA_acre_cherwell_embankment]. Removing or setting back levees lowered flood levels: by 0.66 m on average along a reach, 50 cm on the Elbe and 0.3 m on the Dutch Rhine [ev_flood_hazard_jacob15_1, ev_flood_hazard_serra22_1, ev_flood_hazard_knox22_4]. A meta-analysis finds that on average wetlands reduce flood frequency and size [ev_flood_hazard_kad16_1]. In a Canadian basin model, restored wetland eased the rise in spring flood peaks [ev_wet_eff_goy22_1].
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: The class is low: the clear evidence is local and for moderate storms. In extreme floods and at large catchment scale there is little or no effect [ev_wetflA_dads_summary_extreme_null, ev_wetflA_dads_largecatchment_null]; the same hollow wetlands held 41% of a 100-year storm, and at a catchment outlet the modelled peak fell by only 0.65% to 1.1% [ev_wetflA_acre_depression_storage, ev_flood_hazard_worl23_2, ev_flood_hazard_worl23_3]. Measured studies show smaller effects than models [ev_flood_hazard_kad16_2]. Position can reverse the effect: upstream wetland raised downstream risk in a Chinese basin, restoring some reaches worsened flooding upstream, and Zimbabwean headwater dambos were found to generate storm runoff [ev_flood_hazard_wu23_4, ev_flood_hazard_gour20_4, ev_wetflA_acre_dambo_reversal]. Rewetting can also use up storage space floods would need [ev_wetflA_acre_somerset_rewet_cost]. Much evidence is about existing wetlands: a modelled Indonesian comparison found intact peat flooded less (5%) than degraded peat (25%) in a very wet year [ev_flood_hazard_page09_5]. The corpus is mostly temperate and high-income, and the benefit is off the farm.
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.agreement_note: Most sources show lower peaks or levels near the works; many show no effect in big floods, and six report flooding made worse depending on position [ev_flood_hazard_wu23_4, ev_flood_hazard_gour20_4, ev_wetflA_acre_dambo_reversal, ev_flood_hazard_bull03_3].
