wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: Wetlands feed nearby households through crops and fish. After pilot flood releases on the Waza Logone floodplain in Cameroon, each fishing household caught on average 29 sacks of wet fish a year instead of 15 [ev_fish_catch_loth04_2], and the project book says the floods make a major contribution to local food security [ev_food_security_loth04_6]. In Uganda households report getting about half of their food from wetlands [ev_wet_foodsec_tury13_2], and in Laos farmers said protected fish zones give them more food [ev_wgy_lao_4].
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: Only the Cameroon catch is a change after restoration, and it is a project's own grey-literature account with no comparison area [ev_fish_catch_loth04_2]. The other gains describe what households take from existing wetlands [ev_wet_foodsec_tury13_2, ev_wgy_lao_4, ev_food_security_loth04_6]. In the Uganda survey, households collecting wetland products were more likely to be food insecure [ev_wet_foodsec_tury13_1], and a matched evaluation of a Ugandan restoration project, which restricted wetland access, found no significant food-security change [ev_food_security_fp034e_4]. Benefits follow where restoration keeps or opens household use of the wetland, and are at risk where it closes access.
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.agreement_note: Most sources point to food gains; the Uganda survey finds higher food insecurity among wetland users and the Uganda evaluation finds no change [ev_wet_foodsec_tury13_1, ev_food_security_fp034e_4].

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: Returning floods to grazing land improves pasture: after pilot flood releases on the Waza Logone floodplain in Cameroon, the breeding rate of cows rose from 16% to 50% [ev_livestock_productivity_loth04_1], and reopening a creek in Ghana enhanced cattle farming [ev_livestock_productivity_ghppar_2]. A review of African floodplains shows the other side: where floods are lost, floodplains dry out and stop producing dry-season forage [ev_forage_productivity_fyn15_1, ev_forage_productivity_fyn15_2].
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: The Cameroon gain is a project's own grey-literature account with no comparison area [ev_livestock_productivity_loth04_1]. Near Poyang Lake in China, tenant farmers' crops are damaged by protected birds with no compensation [ev_wgy_poy_2]. A matched Uganda evaluation found no significant yield change [ev_crop_yield_fp034e_5]. Restored wetlands also store less soil nitrogen than reference wetlands for decades [ev_soil_nitrogen_mm12_4], an ecological shortfall rather than a farm loss.
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.agreement_note: Livestock gains where floods return; crop damage near a protected lake [ev_wgy_poy_2] and no change in Uganda [ev_crop_yield_fp034e_5].

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: For the restoration and rewetting family the one recurring figure is upkeep expressed against the build: annual monitoring costs are typically around 20% of the initial restoration investment for floodplain restoration in the USA, and mangrove restoration in the Philippines and Vietnam [ev_project_cost_tail20w1_11].
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: A single source carries this row, and the figure is a cited summary in a cost-effectiveness review rather than a measurement from named projects. It is a share of the initial investment, not an amount: what it costs in money depends entirely on the establishment cost it trails. The named settings are the USA, the Philippines and Vietnam, and the mangrove cases belong to a practice now tracked as its own category, so for wetland rewetting proper the floodplain case is the only anchor.

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: Restoring floodplains and lakebeds has been found both to lower and to raise household income. It falls where farmland is retired: at Poyang Lake income fell, and 56.9% of households said it decreased, blamed on low compensation [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_2, ev_wgy_poy_1]; a Uganda evaluation found lower total income [ev_household_income_fp034e_2]; and US landowners restoring wetland earn only about 18% of farming returns from existing markets [ev_economic_return_jenk10_5]. It rises where floods return to resources people use: in Cameroon, fish catch per household nearly doubled and the floodplain gained an estimated 4,360 euros per square kilometre a year [ev_fish_catch_loth04_2, ev_economic_return_loth04_5]. Transfers and wages add smaller gains [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_4, ev_household_income_bbr_3].
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: What separates the sides is whether restoration takes land or access away, or gives back resources such as fish and pasture, and whether payment replaces what is lost [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_2, ev_fish_catch_loth04_2]. The Cameroon gains are a project's own grey-literature valuation [ev_economic_return_loth04_5]. US wetlands repaying public costs within a year is a society-level return, held out of the class [ev_economic_return_jenk10_4]. The Poyang loss was no longer significant in a later round [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_7]. A European review comparing restoration costs with values for wetland services taken from other studies puts the benefit to society at more than 4,000 euros per hectare a year, against a restoration cost of about 227 euros per hectare a year [ev_economic_return_strz25_4]; this is a return to society, not to households, so it is held out of the rating.

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: Wetlands hold water and slow it, which keeps it from cutting into the land. At the Manalana wetland in South Africa's Sand River catchment, rehabilitation structures halted actively advancing erosion gullies that would otherwise have continued through the wetland and degraded the entire area (ev_erosion_hazard_bbr_1). A weighted meta-analysis of the flow-regulation services of wetlands (Kadykalo et al.) adds the water side: on average wetlands decrease runoff and streamflow (ev_runoff_reduction_kad16_1).
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: The class is slight and carries no strength: neither unit measures soil loss. The Manalana result is a programme narrative from a sustainable-development case study, with no measurement of gully extent or sediment, and it concerns gullies cutting through the wetland itself rather than erosion on the farmland around it (ev_erosion_hazard_bbr_1). The meta-analysis compares existing wetlands with drained or absent ones, mostly in North America and Europe, and reports runoff and streamflow, not erosion; less runoff is a route to less erosion, not a measure of it (ev_runoff_reduction_kad16_1). A measured erosion or sediment-yield finding after a wetland is rehabilitated would let this row say how much.

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: Reinstating wetland water puts nutrient-laden water back in contact with wet soil and plants. Restored or constructed wetlands retained a median 31.4% of total phosphorus and 28.6% of phosphate [ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_3, ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_4]. Modelled floodplain reconnection met a watershed's phosphorus target [ev_nutrient_removal_worl23_5]. Restoring US farmland to forested wetland removed about 36 kg of nitrate per hectare a year at first, rising to almost 68 [ev_nutrient_removal_jenk10_2]; Moldova's rehabilitated Lapusna wetland is estimated to retain about 17 tons of nitrogen a year [ev_nutrient_removal_mdicr_1].
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: On former drained cropland the phosphorus benefit can reverse into a small net release [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_7]. 16% of wetland site-years released more phosphorus than they received, most often in restored wetlands with rain-driven inflow [ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_1, ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_7]. Early US nitrate gains come mainly from taking land out of crops [ev_nutrient_removal_jenk10_2]; the floodplain result is modelled and the Moldovan figure an estimate. No low-income evidence.
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.agreement_note: Most sources show nutrient removal; some show phosphorus release [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_7, ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_1].

wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.mechanism: Wetlands store rain and release it slowly [ev_wet_water_regulation_ramsar18_1]. A meta-analysis finds wetlands on average support low flows [ev_water_regulation_kad16_1]. In Lao PDR a weir doubled the farmland able to use wetland water [ev_wgy_lao_1]; in Belarus managed water levels kept a fen close to its target [ev_wgy_blr_5]; and in Cameroon restored floods refilled waterholes, shortening the distance livestock walk to water [ev_water_access_deficit_loth04_3].
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.conditionality: The class is moderate. A global review of existing wetlands found headwater wetlands more often increase than reduce flow swings [ev_water_regulation_bull03_13]. Field studies found no significant gain in floodplain storage where models showed one [ev_wetflA_zhu_restoration_variability]. The Lao gain comes from a weir, the Belarus levels depend on ongoing regulation, and the Cameroon result is grey literature [ev_wgy_lao_1, ev_wgy_blr_5, ev_water_access_deficit_loth04_3].
wetland_management__restoration_rewettin.agreement_note: Most sources point to more water held; headwater wetlands often add to flow swings [ev_water_regulation_bull03_13].

wetland_management__rural_poverty.mechanism: Household income has been found both to rise and to fall with wetland management. It falls where farmland is taken out of use: at Poyang Lake, households that returned farmland to the lake saw income fall [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_2, ev_wgy_poy_1]; a Uganda project evaluation found lower total income among project households [ev_household_income_fp034e_2]; German farms rewetting grassland lost on average 35% of gross margin [ev_wet_hhinc_meye26_1]; in the US, carbon and hunting markets pay landowners only about 18% of farming returns [ev_economic_return_jenk10_5]; and in Indonesia existing livelihoods will no longer be feasible on rewetted peat [ev_wet_eff_yuwa21_5]. It rises through payments, wages and products that sell: compensation transfers at Poyang, restoration jobs in South Africa, and high-value products such as thatching reed [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_4, ev_household_income_bbr_3, ev_wet_econret_neud26_2]. German fen wet pastures with hardy breeds were profitable in all scenarios [ev_economic_return_tann22_4]. In Cameroon, restored floods nearly doubled household fish catches and added an estimated 4,360 euros per square kilometre a year [ev_fish_catch_loth04_2, ev_economic_return_loth04_5]. In South Sumatra, a cited study found native peat-swamp trees (Shorea balangeran and Dyera polyphylla) worth more than the current practice of burning to plant sonor rice [ev_wet_econret_budi20_2].
wetland_management__rural_poverty.conditionality: What separates the sides is who bears the cost and how it is replaced. Losses come where farmland or wetland access is taken away and compensation is small or absent [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_2, ev_wgy_poy_1]; gains come from wages, compensation, new livelihoods and niche products [ev_household_income_bbr_3, ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_4, ev_wet_econret_neud26_2]. Several gains go to society, not households, and are held out of the class: a restored fen at Wicken Fen has a benefit-cost ratio of 4.4 against 1.3 for farming, and restored US wetlands repay public costs within a year, but both count climate and other public benefits [ev_economic_return_rgwo25_1, ev_economic_return_jenk10_4]. The Cameroon and Chinese ecotourism gains are project accounts in grey literature [ev_economic_return_loth04_5, ev_economic_return_rgwo25_7]. The South Sumatra comparison is second-hand and gives no figure [ev_wet_econret_budi20_2]. A European review comparing restoration costs with values for wetland services taken from other studies puts the benefit to society at more than 4,000 euros per hectare a year, against a restoration cost of about 227 euros per hectare a year [ev_economic_return_strz25_4]; this is a return to society, not to households, so it is held out of the rating.

wetland_management__rural_poverty__aez-h.mechanism: All the units here concern wet use of tropical peat and come from reviews citing other work. On the gain side, sago, a crop that grows on shallow peat without drainage, is cited at an internal rate of return of 12.9–19%, rising to 17.4–19.2% once environmental benefits are counted [ev_economic_return_tan21_9], and the same review concludes from NPV, IRR and BCR that paludiculture may generate a small margin of economic benefit, while adding in the same sentence that its benefits relative to conventional drainage-based crops are still too low and that not all costs and externalities are documented [ev_economic_return_tan21_10]. On the loss side, communities that have relied on oil palm cultivation will find it challenging to participate in peatland restoration, since rewetting may entail lower productivity and financial return for their crops [ev_household_income_mish21_5].
wetland_management__rural_poverty__aez-h.conditionality: The direction is a slight gain carried by modelled returns to a wet crop, and the loss for oil-palm households is kept as harm to those adopters, not averaged away. What separates them is the starting point: a household that can grow and sell sago or another wet crop gains a modest return, while a household giving up drained oil palm loses income relative to what it had. Neither review measures a household or attaches a magnitude to the loss, the sago returns are cited from other studies with no inflation adjustment, and the oil-palm finding comes from a bundled rewetting and revegetation programme. Both sources describe Indonesian and Malaysian upper-middle-income settings, so a low- or lower-middle-income humid-tropics investment has no directly applicable evidence here, and compensation or a payment is likely to be needed where drained plantation crops are retired.

wetland_management__rural_poverty__farmi.mechanism: Where rainfed cropland is withdrawn for restoration, household income has been found to fall and, through payments or wages, to rise. At Poyang Lake, per capita income fell by 0.338 log points for households that returned farmland to the lake, with the authors reporting a significant negative impact on income, while total, farm and non-agricultural income fell without reaching significance [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_1, ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_3, ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_5] and transfer income rose (ATT 0.717) [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_2, ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_6, ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_4]. In South Africa, Working for Wetlands employed people previously without stable income to rehabilitate wetlands, and at Manalana a cost-benefit analysis set provisioning benefits to local households against rehabilitation cost [ev_household_income_bbr_3, ev_economic_return_bbr_2]. In Central Kalimantan, modelled crops grown with no drainage or shallow drainage put dragon fruit, candlenut and mangosteen at NPVs of more than €40,000/ha, comparable to oil palm [ev_wet_econret_uda20_1], and mature sago stands in Riau are cited at revenues of up to 1500 euro per ha per year [ev_wet_econret_uda20_2]. In Kabale, Uganda, the wetland policy had little impact on household incomes [ev_wet_hhinc_masa22_1].
wetland_management__rural_poverty__farmi.conditionality: The sides differ in channel: the loss is lost harvest from retired cropland, the gains are compensation transfers and public-works wages rather than income from the restored wetland [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_2, ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_4, ev_household_income_bbr_3]. The Kalimantan gains are a different channel again, a saleable crop that tolerates a high water table, but they are modelled, exclude the cost of the rewetting works, and the most profitable crop in the set still needs some drainage [ev_wet_econret_uda20_1]; sago, the true wet crop, takes years to first harvest [ev_wet_econret_uda20_2]. Payments sized to replace the lost harvest, or a wet crop with a market, are therefore the design condition. The Poyang loss faded to non-significance years after the policy began [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_7]. On quality, the Poyang matched study dominates the weight and describes an upper-middle-income lakebed-retirement programme; its transfer gain is a component of income whose total fell, not an independent finding. In Kabale 22% of respondents get no income at all from the wetlands, which describes existing use rather than a change from restoration and is not read as a restoration effect [ev_wet_hhinc_masa22_3]. A Central Kalimantan report of income losses after a fire ban was rejected at review by Pete Steward, who was not confident it could be included, and is no longer counted here.

wetland_management__rural_poverty__incom.mechanism: In high-income settings, farm income on rewetted land has been found both to fall and to hold up, depending on what is sold. Wet farming is generally not profitable on biomass sales alone, and income is hard to keep at the conventional level [ev_wet_econret_neud26_1, ev_wet_econret_temm26_4]. German farms rewetting grassland lost on average 35% of gross margin [ev_wet_hhinc_meye26_1], and US landowners restoring wetland earn from carbon and hunting only about 18% of farming returns [ev_economic_return_jenk10_5]. On the other side, thatching reed and directly sold buffalo products can pay [ev_wet_econret_neud26_2], German fen wet pastures with hardy breeds were profitable in all scenarios [ev_economic_return_tann22_4], and Australian cane farmers building lagoons had benefit-cost ratios of 0.8 to 1.5, higher when raised land could grow cane [ev_wet_eff_cann22_3].
wetland_management__rural_poverty__incom.conditionality: Product and payment separate the sides: bulk biomass loses while niche products and payment-backed systems can pay [ev_wet_econret_neud26_1, ev_wet_econret_neud26_2]. The German wet-farming profits include agri-environment payments [ev_economic_return_tann22_4], and the Australian lagoons were subsidised [ev_wet_eff_cann22_3]. Society-level returns are held out of the class: Wicken Fen's benefit-cost ratio of 4.4 against 1.3 for farming, and US wetlands repaying public costs within a year, both count public benefits [ev_economic_return_rgwo25_1, ev_economic_return_jenk10_4]. Most results are modelled. A European review comparing restoration costs with values for wetland services taken from other studies puts the benefit to society at more than 4,000 euros per hectare a year, against a restoration cost of about 227 euros per hectare a year [ev_economic_return_strz25_4]; this is a return to society, not to households, so it is held out of the rating.

wetland_management__rural_poverty__incom.mechanism: The matched evidence in low-income settings shows no household gain. The Uganda GCF evaluation found that awareness, crop diversification and adaptation changes did not translate into measurable improvements in income or asset accumulation; total income was lower among treated households, significant at the 10 per cent level, while crop-farming income was close to zero difference [ev_household_income_fp034e_1, ev_household_income_fp034e_2, ev_household_income_fp034e_3]. In Kabale, Uganda, the national wetland policy had little impact on household incomes [ev_wet_hhinc_masa22_1], and 22% of respondents earned no income at all from the wetlands, leaving them no incentive to conserve, a statement about existing use rather than a change from restoration [ev_wet_hhinc_masa22_3]. The only gain is reported in Uzbekistan, where the revival of fish, muskrat skin and reed production from wetlands formed by the project contributed to a substantial increase in income for residents [ev_household_income_uzicr_1].
wetland_management__rural_poverty__incom.conditionality: The sides are a matched evaluation and a completion-report assertion, and they differ in what the wetland gave households. The loss is in Uganda, where rehabilitation came with restrictions on cultivation inside demarcated wetlands alongside livelihood packages, and treated households had lower total income at endline, significant only at the 10 per cent level, while crop-farming income showed close to zero difference [ev_household_income_fp034e_2, ev_household_income_fp034e_3]. The gain is in Uzbekistan, where new wetlands formed along drainage collectors revived harvestable fish, muskrat skin and reeds; the completion report asserts the income increase rather than measuring it [ev_household_income_uzicr_1]. The separator is whether the wetland opens a product households can sell or closes land they farmed. Most of the weight is neither: the Uganda evaluation found no measurable improvement in income or asset accumulation, and the Kabale policy had little impact on household incomes [ev_household_income_fp034e_1, ev_wet_hhinc_masa22_1]. Treat restoration in low-income settings as income-neutral to negative unless the design adds an adequate, well-targeted livelihood payment or product channel.

wetland_management__rural_poverty__incom.mechanism: In upper-middle-income settings, household income has been found both to fall and to rise with wetland restoration. Losses follow land taken out of farming and the size of compensation: at Poyang Lake, households that returned farmland to the lake saw per capita income fall by 0.338 log points, with the authors reporting a significant negative impact [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_2, ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_6] while total, farm and non-agricultural income fell without reaching significance [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_1, ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_3, ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_5], and 56.9% of surveyed households said income decreased after joining the compensation policy, attributed to low compensation rates [ev_wgy_poy_1]; in SE Asia, communities relying on oil palm face lower productivity and financial return under rewetting [ev_household_income_mish21_5]. Gains come through other channels: the same Poyang households gained transfer income (ATT 0.717) [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_4]; Working for Wetlands in South Africa employed people previously without stable income [ev_household_income_bbr_3, ev_economic_return_bbr_2]; tropical paludiculture may generate a small margin of economic benefit [ev_economic_return_tan21_10]; and in Belarus indirect benefits reached agro-ecotourism businesses and wild-berry marketing [ev_wgy_blr_2]. Newer project accounts add to the gain side: in Viet Nam's U Minh Thuong buffer zone, Green Contracts for alternative fire-free income sources resulted in a doubling of annual incomes [ev_wet_hhinc_terz22_1]; in Riau, 75% of the 152 respondents registered monthly income increase of more than USD 35 from selling community-garden harvest [ev_wet_hhinc_terz22_2]; and in South Sumatra fishponds inside a rewetted canal system generated 18,700,000 IDR from the 2019 harvest, which the authors call not yet optimal [ev_wet_hhinc_budi20_1]. Paludiculture crops now count for the peatland family, and they add to the gain side, all modelled or second-hand: sago's internal rate of return is cited at 12.9–19%, rising to 17.4–19.2% when environmental benefits are counted [ev_economic_return_tan21_9]; in Central Kalimantan, dragon fruit, candlenut and mangosteen were modelled at NPVs of more than €40,000/ha, comparable to oil palm [ev_wet_econret_uda20_1]; mature sago stands in Riau are cited at revenues of up to 1500 euro per ha per year [ev_wet_econret_uda20_2]; and water spinach in a South Sumatran agro-sylvofishery project had a benefit-cost ratio of 2.97 by the project manager's account [ev_wet_econret_budi20_1].
wetland_management__rural_poverty__incom.conditionality: What separates the sides is the channel: households lose where farmland or drained-peat crops are given up and compensation is small or absent, and gain through transfers, wages on restoration works, or local businesses [ev_wgy_poy_1, ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_4, ev_household_income_bbr_3, ev_wgy_blr_2]. Time also matters: the Poyang loss was no longer significant by the later panel round [ev_wet_hhinc_feng24_7]. Product is a further separator: crops that grow on wet or shallow-drained peat and find a market carry the modelled gains [ev_economic_return_tan21_9, ev_wet_econret_uda20_2]. Compensation size, who receives it, and whether a saleable wet crop is built in are the levers a project controls. The crop gains are weaker than they look: the Kalimantan model excludes the cost of restoring drained peat, such as canal dams, and its most profitable crop, dragon fruit, still needs some drainage [ev_wet_econret_uda20_1]; the sago revenue is for mature stands that take years to reach first harvest [ev_wet_econret_uda20_2]; the sago returns are cited from other studies [ev_economic_return_tan21_9]; and the water-spinach ratio is a project figure for a community demonstration, not a household income [ev_wet_econret_budi20_1]. On quality, the losses include matched household estimates, while the gains are weaker as household evidence: the Poyang transfer gain is a component of income whose total fell, the tropical paludiculture margin is small and, by the authors' caveat, still too low against drainage-based crops [ev_economic_return_tan21_10], the Belarus benefits did not explicitly reach vulnerable groups, and the Chinese high-altitude peatland claim that restoration helps alleviate poverty is an editorial forward reference, not a measured result [ev_rural_poverty_bonn16_3]. Belarus found no direct household benefit because none was designed [ev_wgy_blr_1]. A Central Kalimantan report of income losses in villages that had stopped fire use was rejected at review by Pete Steward, who was not confident it could be included, and is no longer counted; the row stays split without it. The Vietnamese and Riau gains come from alternative livelihoods bundled with the restoration rather than from the restored peat, are self-reported and have no comparison group [ev_wet_hhinc_terz22_1, ev_wet_hhinc_terz22_2], and the Sumatran fish income is a community demonstration-project total, not a household figure [ev_wet_hhinc_budi20_1]. The Indonesian social cost-benefit results are held out of the class as societal welfare with carbon priced in: enhanced rewetting with paludiculture yielded a lower average NPV over 25 years but a higher average NPV over 50 years [ev_wet_econret_jali25_1], and paludiculture restoration offered superior ecosystem services compared with oil-palm monoculture [ev_wet_econret_jali25_3].

wetland_management__soil_erosion_risk.mechanism: Vegetation and wetland structures hold soil and sediment in place, and the result is clearest for coastal marsh. Against a degraded shore, salt-marsh planting enhances shoreline protection, which the meta-analysis measures as vertical accretion, elevation change, sediment deposition and shoreline change rates (effect size 0.61) (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_3). A meta-analysis of China's coastal wetland restoration (Liu et al.) found coastal stabilization - indicators such as vertical accretion rate - significantly improved in restored against degraded wetlands, by 19.7 % (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_1). In the restoration sub-practice, South Africa's Manalana wetland is the only case: rehabilitation structures halted the advance of erosion gullies that would otherwise have continued throughout the wetland and degraded the entire area (ev_erosion_hazard_bbr_1).
wetland_management__soil_erosion_risk.conditionality: The class is moderate, and its strength comes from the coastal units: it concerns shoreline protection and coastal stabilization against a degraded marsh or coast, not soil loss from fields. The 0.61 effect size is on a scale the source does not define (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_3); the Chinese figure is a pooled response ratio across restoration types that include building dikes as well as planting (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_1). The peatland evidence is a single runoff-volume unit, not an erosion measurement: at a blanket-peat restoration, the share of storm rainfall becoming storm discharge did not change at either restored site relative to the bare control (ev_wetflA_shut_runoffcoef_null), the paper concluding that restoration shifted the timing and peak of delivery rather than the volume - a null that says the peatland evidence here does not speak to erosion. The Manalana gully result is a programme narrative without a measurement, and it concerns gullies cutting through the wetland itself rather than soil loss from surrounding fields (ev_erosion_hazard_bbr_1). Sediment that a wetland traps from water flowing through it is a water-quality service, not prevention of landscape erosion, and those units vote in the water-quality row, not here. Nothing in the pool measures soil loss on farmland, and apart from the South African case all of it comes from high- and upper-middle-income coastal and upland settings.

wetland_management__soil_erosion_risk__f.mechanism: A wetland in a farmed catchment can hold soil in two ways: rehabilitation structures stop gullies cutting into the wetland, and a wetland in the flow path traps sediment carried from upstream. In South Africa's Manalana wetland, rehabilitation halted actively advancing erosion gullies that would otherwise have continued through the wetland and degraded the entire area (ev_erosion_hazard_bbr_1). At created riverine wetlands in Ohio, the trapping service is what the evidence tracks, and there are some signs that sediment and total phosphorus retention are diminishing after 10 years of river flow (ev_sediment_retention_mits05_5).
wetland_management__soil_erosion_risk__f.conditionality: Neither unit measures soil loss on cropland, and the adverse direction of this row comes from the Ohio unit, which records a trapping service weakening with age, not a wetland adding erosion: the basins were still retaining sediment, with nitrate and soluble reactive phosphorus retention holding, so the finding is that sediment trapping cannot be assumed to last without maintenance (ev_sediment_retention_mits05_5). The South African unit points the other way but is a programme narrative without a measurement, about gullies in the wetland itself (ev_erosion_hazard_bbr_1). Read together they say a wetland can protect itself from gullying and can trap sediment for a decade or so; they say nothing about erosion on the surrounding rainfed fields.

wetland_management__soil_erosion_risk__i.mechanism: In high-income settings the evidence is about shorelines. Against a degraded shore, planting salt marsh enhances shoreline protection - measured as vertical accretion, elevation change, sediment deposition and shoreline change rates - with an effect size of 0.61 in a global meta-analysis of planting success (Liu et al.) (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_3): the planted canopy slows water so sediment settles and the edge holds.
wetland_management__soil_erosion_risk__i.conditionality: The class is slight and carries no strength, because the 0.61 effect size is on a scale the abstract does not define, so it is not banded (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_3). It concerns shoreline protection on planted salt marsh, mostly Spartina and mostly in North America, not soil loss from cropland or rangeland. The only other unit is a runoff-volume null at an English blanket-peat restoration: the share of storm rainfall becoming storm discharge did not change at either restored site relative to the bare control (ev_wetflA_shut_runoffcoef_null); it measures runoff, not erosion, and restoration there shifted the timing and peak of delivery rather than the volume. No unit measures erosion on farmland, and none comes from a lower-income country.

wetland_management__water_quality_risk.mechanism: Water moving slowly through a created or restored wetland drops sediment, and plants and soil microbes remove nutrients. Across created and restored wetlands, median removal was 37% of incoming nitrogen and 46% of phosphorus [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_3, ev_nutrient_removal_land16_4]. Restored or constructed wetlands retained a median 31.4% of total phosphorus [ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_3]. Restoring US farmland to forested wetland removed about 36 kg of nitrate per hectare a year at first, rising to almost 68 [ev_nutrient_removal_jenk10_2]. Placing wetlands where nitrogen surplus is highest gives about 40 times more removal than placing them on non-farm land [ev_nutrient_removal_cheng20_4].
wetland_management__water_quality_risk.conditionality: The phosphorus benefit can reverse on the land this tool targets: wetlands restored on former drained cropland showed a small net release of phosphorus [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_7]. Across 273 wetland site-years, 16% released more phosphorus than they received, most often in restored wetlands with rain-driven inflow [ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_1, ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_7]. Rewetting fertilised farm fens may release stored nutrients [ev_wgy_ram_9]. Early US nitrate gains come mainly from taking land out of crops [ev_nutrient_removal_jenk10_2]. Evidence is mostly high-income; strip or isolate phosphorus-rich topsoil where possible.
wetland_management__water_quality_risk.agreement_note: Most sources show nutrient removal; several show phosphorus release on former cropland, in rain-fed restored wetlands or rewetted fens [ev_nutrient_removal_land16_7, ev_nutrient_removal_ury23w1_1, ev_wgy_ram_9].

wetland_management__water_quality_risk__.mechanism: In rainfed cropping catchments a wetland works as an interception point for the nutrients leaving the fields. In the 10th year after construction, average nitrate removal by the created riverine basins was 42%, the highest of the decade [ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_1], and soluble reactive phosphorus retention continued to be significant at around 70%, 63% in the planted basin and 73% in the naturally colonising one, with no significant difference between them [ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_2]. In Swedish farmland, nutrient retention and diversity proved compatible aims, since biodiversity was neither locally nor regionally harmed by high nitrate levels [ev_nutrient_removal_thie09_6].
wetland_management__water_quality_risk__.conditionality: Phosphorus is where this fails. By the 10th year total phosphorus showed little retention and even export, falling by only 2% in the naturally colonising basin and rising by 14% in the planted one, after a consistent pattern of retention over the first 8 years [ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_3, ev_nutrient_removal_mits05_4]: the created wetland had become a net phosphorus exporter in its tenth year. Sediment and total phosphorus retention were diminishing after 10 years of river flow [ev_sediment_retention_mits05_5], so the particulate fraction of the service decays as the basin fills while the dissolved-nutrient service persists. Both studies sit in temperate, high-income rainfed cropland, Ohio and Sweden, and both concern created wetlands fed by river or catchment water rather than restored ones; the Ohio basins were continuously pumped, which is not how a wetland in a farmed catchment is fed. Nothing was measured in a tropical or lower-income rainfed system.

wetland_management__water_quality_risk__.mechanism: Water slowed and spread through a rehabilitated wetland drops sediment and gives plants and soil time to take up and transform nutrients. On Moldova's rehabilitated Lapusna wetland, estimated annual nutrient retention is about 17 tons N and 3.0 tons P, assuming an average annual flow through of 10,600,000m3 [ev_nutrient_removal_mdicr_1]. On the Chinese coast, a meta-analysis of coastal wetland restoration (Liu et al.) found water purification and waste treatment indicators significantly improved against degraded wetlands, by 69.3 % [ev_nutrient_removal_liu24_1].
wetland_management__water_quality_risk__.conditionality: The strong class rests on both units agreeing, not on depth of evidence, and each has limits. The Moldovan figure is a project completion report's own estimate from inlet and outlet sampling over part of a year, scaled by an assumed flow, with no pre-restoration or unrestored reference [ev_nutrient_removal_mdicr_1]. The Chinese figure is a pooled response ratio for a broad water-purification category across coastal restoration types, from planting mangroves to breaking dikes, not a measured nutrient load [ev_nutrient_removal_liu24_1]. Neither concerns a wetland restored on former cropland, which is where phosphorus release is reported elsewhere in the wetland evidence, and both settings - a river-fed Ramsar wetland and the Chinese coast - are upper-middle-income, so the transfer to a low-income farmed catchment is untested.

wetland_management__water_stress.mechanism: Wetlands store rain and release it slowly [ev_wet_water_regulation_ramsar18_1]. After restoration, water tables rose on Exmoor peat and on drained extraction sites [ev_wetflA_gatis_watertable, ev_water_regulation_rasa23_6], and canal dams in Indonesian peat kept the water table above the fire-risk level through a dry year [ev_water_regulation_doh18_1]. In Lao PDR a weir doubled the farmland able to use wetland water, from 37.16 ha to 73.47 ha [ev_wgy_lao_1], and in Cameroon restored floods refilled natural waterholes so livestock had shorter distances to drinking water [ev_water_access_deficit_loth04_3].
wetland_management__water_stress.conditionality: The class is moderate because few results give a size, and most gains are inside the wetland. Restored peat often regains its level but not its natural ups and downs, and many processes take years to recover [ev_water_regulation_rasa23_7, ev_wetflA_acre_recovery_timescale]. Field studies found no significant gain in floodplain water storage where models showed one [ev_wetflA_zhu_restoration_variability]. The Lao gain comes from a weir, not restoration, and the Cameroon result is a project's own grey-literature observation [ev_wgy_lao_1, ev_water_access_deficit_loth04_3].
wetland_management__water_stress.agreement_note: Most sources point to more water held; some find no significant change [ev_wetflA_zhu_restoration_variability, ev_water_regulation_rasa23_7].

wetland_management__water_stress__income.mechanism: In the high-income boreo-temperate evidence, rewetting measurably puts water back where the drain took it from. On an eroding English upland peatland, peat barriers across gullies raised mean water tables significantly at all distance classes, in the peat pans from 0.003 m below ground level to 0.064 m above it and in the vegetated haggs from 0.188 to 0.175 m below ground within 0.5 m of the pan edge [ev_wetflA_gatis_watertable]. On cutaway peat, the water-table level was successfully recovered by active restoration through ditch blocking and dam construction [ev_water_regulation_rasa23_6]. A basin-scale model of rewetting drained peat in the Neman basin (Stachowicz et al.) puts the extra water retained at 69 to 344 m3·ha−1, or 23.6–118 M m3 across the basin [ev_water_regulation_sta22_1].
wetland_management__water_stress__income.conditionality: The recovery is partial. The near-ditch groundwater evidence, with its small footprint and inconclusive effects outside the wetland soil, now sits in the catchment water yield rows. The English rise is in the mean rather than the typical state: median water-table conditions remained similar at all distances after restoration, so the significant mean rise is driven by the wet tail [ev_wetflA_gatis_watertable]. Water-table fluctuation and the moisture dynamics of the peat layer were difficult to maintain in restored peat-extraction areas, so the level returns but its dynamics do not [ev_water_regulation_rasa23_7]. Catchment storage is contested: a fieldwork-based study found no significant increase in floodplain water storage or overland flow, while modelling showed a 6-fold increase in overland flow storage volume, and the fieldwork study is itself cited within this review rather than independent of it [ev_wetflA_zhu_restoration_variability]. The Neman model is a scenario estimate, and its basin total corresponds to 0.14–0.7% of the total annual Neman River discharge into the Baltic Sea - water held in the peat, not delivered to users [ev_water_regulation_sta22_1]. Every unit is temperate or boreal, from the UK, Ireland, Fennoscandia, Canada and the Neman basin, and none measures water available to a farming system.

wetland_management__water_stress__income.mechanism: In Lao PDR, a weir at the Nongdern wetland doubled the farmland able to draw wetland water, from 37.16 ha to 73.47 ha [ev_wgy_lao_1], and renovating dykes refilled previously dry lakes for the dry season [ev_wgy_lao_2]. In Cameroon, restored floods refilled natural waterholes, so livestock and wildlife had shorter distances to drinking water [ev_water_access_deficit_loth04_3].
wetland_management__water_stress__income.conditionality: The Lao gain comes from water-control works inside a wetland, not from restoring wetland function, and the dyke result is the evaluators' conclusion [ev_wgy_lao_1, ev_wgy_lao_2]. The Cameroon result is a project's own grey-literature observation with no measurement [ev_water_access_deficit_loth04_3]. These are single sites.
wetland_management__water_stress__income.agreement_note: All three sources point to more water available.

wetland_management__water_stress__income.mechanism: There is not enough evidence to rate this. Ramsar guidance states that wetlands store water from rain and slowly release it, which can recharge groundwater and maintain the water cycle [ev_wet_water_regulation_ramsar18_1]. A review adds that many studies of peat rewetting suggest water processes do not fully recover within the first few years after restoration, because of earlier damage to the peat [ev_wetflA_acre_recovery_timescale].
wetland_management__water_stress__income.conditionality: Neither finding is a measured result of restoration. The Ramsar statement describes wetlands in general, with no size, timing or country [ev_wet_water_regulation_ramsar18_1], and the review's point is about how long recovery takes [ev_wetflA_acre_recovery_timescale]. Nothing here measures water supply for farms. A measured change in water availability downstream of a restored wetland is needed before a rating can be given.

wetland_management__waterlogging__all.mechanism: Rewetting can make waterlogging worse on neighbouring land; how much is not known. Raising the water table in the peat does not stop at the project boundary. Ramsar technical guidance on peatland rewetting says that where nearby land use may be harmed, rewetting must be done gradually and flooding of surrounding land avoided [ev_wgy_ram_15], and that where water seeps diffusely downward, raising the water table in the remaining peat will require raising the water level in the surrounding land, farmland included [ev_wgy_ram_16]. A UK review of rewetting farmed peat adds that changing one part of a drainage system can have unintended effects on neighbouring land, flooding land and property the rewetting programme did not mean to flood [ev_waterlogging_hazard_cxc21_1].
wetland_management__waterlogging__all.conditionality: All three statements are expert judgement from guidance and a review, not measurements: none says how often neighbouring land is waterlogged, by how much, for how long, or what it costs the farmers who work it [ev_wgy_ram_15, ev_wgy_ram_16, ev_waterlogging_hazard_cxc21_1]. The UK review ties the risk to how well soils, landform and drainage are understood, and notes that not all sites can be rewetted, depending on where they sit in the drainage system [ev_waterlogging_hazard_cxc21_1]. Unlike the flood benefits elsewhere for this practice, this cost falls on the neighbouring farm household rather than downstream. The only country named is the UK, a rich country; the Ramsar guidance names none. What is missing to give a size is a measured observation of waterlogging on farmland next to a rewetted site.

wetland_management__wind_cyclone__all.mechanism: This cell carries no measured wind or cyclone mechanism. Its sole unit is a caution about the asset rather than a protective effect: a replacement wetland may take decades to fully develop the functions provided by the original wetland (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_7). Whatever storm-protection function an established coastal wetland performs, the evidence here says a newly restored or created wetland does not perform it from the outset.
wetland_management__wind_cyclone__all.conditionality: No class is stated. The one unit is an expert statement in the discussion section of a US study, not on a measurement, and it concerns compensatory replacement wetlands rather than any practice sited in a rural landscape. There is no quantified wind or cyclone outcome in scope, no non-high-income setting, and no farm-level beneficiary — the protection at issue is of coastal property. What is missing is a second independent source or one measured finding on storm protection by a restored or created wetland. Until then the row carries a single usable implication: an establishment lag of decades before any protective function can be credited to the works.
